recipes.storage: Keeps 10 days refrigerated, and improves for the first four. Reheat to a full simmer each time, always with a dry spoon, and add a splash of vinegar if it tastes flat.

recipes.name: Sungtachi Kodi
recipes.subtitle: everyday prawn and drumstick curry in a thin red coconut masala

ingredients.note: adds the sweetness that makes this curry
for colour more than heat
or 1 tbsp tamarind pulp

prepNotes: Toss the prawns with 1/4 tsp turmeric and a pinch of salt and leave 15 minutes, then rinse and drain well.
Rinse the kokum petals and soak them in 3 tbsp warm water while you grind the masala.
Peel the drumsticks with a knife, leaving the tender inner rib — the tough outer skin never softens.

steps.text: Grind the coconut, Kashmiri chillies, coriander powder, cumin, turmeric and garlic with 250ml warm water to a completely smooth paste.
steps.tip: Blend for a full four minutes. A gritty masala is the commonest fault in a home coconut curry.

steps.text: Boil the drumstick pieces in 250ml salted water for 8 minutes, until a fingernail marks the flesh easily. Keep the water.
Heat the coconut oil in a wide pan and soften the onion 5 minutes until translucent.
Pour in the ground masala along with the drumstick and its cooking water, add the green chillies and salt, and bring to a simmer.
Simmer 8 minutes, stirring now and then, until the raw smell of the coconut has gone and the curry looks glossy rather than chalky.
steps.tip: Do not let it reach a rolling boil once the coconut is in — it will split.

steps.text: Add the kokum with its soaking water and simmer 2 minutes.
Slide in the prawns and cook 3-4 minutes only, until they curl and turn opaque.
steps.tip: Prawns go from done to rubbery in about a minute. Pull the pan as soon as they curve into a C.

steps.text: Take off the heat, check the salt and sourness, and rest 5 minutes before serving with rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated, though the prawns firm up. Reheat over low heat just to steaming. Do not freeze.

recipes.name: Tondak
recipes.subtitle: dried white peas in a roasted coconut and cashew masala, thick and faintly sweet

ingredients.note: in Goa these would be fresh green cashew in season
whole coriander seed, 1 tbsp, is better if you have it — roast it with the coconut

prepNotes: Soak the white peas overnight in plenty of water — they roughly double, and an under-soaked pea stays chalky no matter how long you cook it.
Soak the cashews separately for 30 minutes so they grind smooth.
Roast the coconut and spices dry before grinding. That roasting is the difference between tondak and an ordinary coconut curry.

steps.text: Pressure cook the drained peas with 400ml water and 1/2 tsp salt for 3 whistles, about 12 minutes, until soft but not split. Keep the cooking water.
steps.tip: Salt the peas from the start — added later it never gets inside them.

steps.text: Dry-roast the grated coconut in a pan over medium heat for 6-8 minutes, stirring constantly, until it turns the colour of weak tea.
steps.tip: It goes from golden to burnt in seconds at the end. Keep the pan moving and pull it early.

steps.text: Add the dried chillies, coriander seeds, cumin, pepper, cloves and cinnamon to the pan and roast 1 minute more, until fragrant.
Grind the roasted coconut and spices with the soaked cashews, turmeric, garlic and 150ml water to a thick, smooth paste.
Heat the coconut oil and fry the chopped onion 8 minutes, until well browned at the edges.
Add the ground masala and fry 6 minutes, stirring, until it thickens and the oil shows at the sides.
Tip in the cooked peas with their water and the remaining water. Simmer 12 minutes.
Stir in the tamarind and jaggery, check the salt, and simmer 5 minutes more until the gravy is thick enough to hold a spoon mark.
steps.tip: Tondak is a thick curry, not a soup. If it looks loose, keep reducing.

steps.text: Rest 10 minutes and serve with rice or pao.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and thickens considerably; loosen with hot water when reheating over low heat. Freezes well for a month.

recipes.name: Bajra no Rotlo
recipes.subtitle: thick hand-patted pearl-millet flatbread, nutty and dense, eaten hot under melting butter

ingredients.note: freshly milled if you can get it; bajra flour goes bitter with age
the classic pairing — rotlo, gud and butter

prepNotes: Bajra has no gluten, so the dough is held together by heat and water alone. Use water as hot as your hands can bear and knead while it is warm.
Mix only as much dough as you will cook in the next twenty minutes. Bajra dough cracks and dries fast, and cold dough will not pat out at all.
Have the tawa heating before you shape the first rotlo — a patted rotlo cannot be moved twice.

steps.text: Warm the flour in a bowl with the salt, then add the hot water in stages, mixing with a spoon at first, then your hand.
Knead 3-4 minutes into a smooth, warm, slightly tacky dough. It should hold a ball without cracking at the edges.
steps.tip: If the edges crack, it is too dry — wet your palm and knead again rather than pouring more water in.

steps.text: Heat a heavy tawa over medium heat until a drop of water skitters across it.
Take a lemon-sized ball, wet your palms, and pat it flat on a clean board or a sheet of plastic, rotating a quarter turn between pats, into a disc about 12cm across and 8mm thick.
steps.tip: Pat with the flat of the fingers in one direction and rotate. Slapping it randomly makes it tear.

steps.text: Lift it on your palm and lay it flat on the hot tawa in one movement.
Cook 90 seconds until the underside is speckled, then flip and cook the second side 2 minutes, pressing the edges with a cloth so it puffs.
Lift the rotlo with tongs and hold it 20-30 seconds directly over the flame, first side down, until it balloons.
steps.tip: It puffs only if both sides are properly cooked first. A rotlo that stays flat is still good — do not chase it over the flame until it burns.

steps.text: Repeat with the rest, stacking them under a cloth.
Serve hot with a knob of butter pressed into the centre and a lump of jaggery, or alongside ringan no olo.

recipes.storage: Rotla are only good hot. Eat within an hour; leftovers can be crumbled the next morning into hot milk with jaggery, which is how Kathiawadi households use them up.

recipes.name: Basundi
recipes.subtitle: milk reduced slowly to a thick grainy cream, scented with cardamom and saffron
prepNotes: Use a wide, heavy-based pan. A narrow deep pot doubles the reduction time and scorches the base.
Rinse the pan with water and pour it out before adding the milk — a wet pan is far less likely to catch.
Set aside a full hour of low-attention stirring. Basundi cannot be hurried on high heat.

steps.text: Bring the milk to a boil in a wide heavy pan over medium heat, stirring so it does not stick.
Lower the heat and simmer, stirring every few minutes and scraping the base each time.
steps.tip: Scrape the base, not just the surface — the burnt taste comes from what settles.

steps.text: As a skin forms at the edges, keep pushing it back into the milk. These layers are what make basundi grainy rather than smooth.
Crush the saffron into 2 tbsp of the hot milk and set it aside to bloom.
Continue reducing for 45-55 minutes, until the milk has come down to about half its volume and coats a spoon thickly.
Add the sugar and cook 8 minutes more; the milk will loosen briefly, then thicken again.
steps.tip: Add sugar only near the end — early sugar makes the milk catch and darken.

steps.text: Stir in the saffron milk, ground cardamom and nutmeg, and take the pan off the heat.
Cool to room temperature, then chill 3 hours; it thickens noticeably as it cools.
steps.tip: Judge the final consistency cold, not hot, or you will over-reduce it.

steps.text: Serve cold in small bowls with the almonds and pistachios scattered over, or warm alongside puris.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated in a covered bowl. Reheat gently over low heat with a splash of milk if you prefer it warm; it thickens further each day.

recipes.name: Bataka Poha
recipes.subtitle: flattened rice tossed with potato, peanuts and lemon, ready in twenty minutes

ingredients.note: thin poha dissolves — it must be the thick kind

ingredients.qty: 2 medium, peeled and cut into 1cm dice

ingredients.note: use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Rinse the poha in a colander under running water for 20 seconds, then leave it to drain for 10 minutes. It should be damp and separate, never sitting in water.
Mix the sugar, salt and turmeric into the drained poha with your fingertips before it goes in the pan — seasoning it in the kadhai always ends up patchy.
Have everything chopped before you start; the whole cook takes under fifteen minutes.

steps.text: Fry the peanuts in the oil over medium heat for 3 minutes until they darken and smell toasted, then lift them out and set aside.
In the same oil pop the mustard seeds, then add the cumin, curry leaves, green chilli and asafoetida.
Add the diced potato, cover, and cook on medium-low 8 minutes, shaking the pan, until tender and lightly golden.
steps.tip: Cover the pan — the potato steams tender without needing more oil.

steps.text: Add the onion and fry 3 minutes until soft and translucent.
Tip in the seasoned poha and fold it through gently with a flat spatula, lifting rather than stirring.
steps.tip: Stirring hard mashes poha into paste. Lift and fold, three or four times only.

steps.text: Cover and steam on the lowest heat 3 minutes, until the poha is hot, plump and pale yellow throughout.
steps.tip: If it looks dry, sprinkle over two tablespoons of water before covering.

steps.text: Turn off the heat, add the lemon juice and the fried peanuts, and fold once.
Scatter the coriander and coconut over and serve hot with a wedge of lemon.

recipes.storage: Best within the hour. Keeps a day refrigerated; revive it in a covered pan over low heat with a sprinkle of water and a fresh squeeze of lemon.

recipes.name: Batata nu Shaak
recipes.subtitle: everyday tomato-tempered potatoes, faintly sweet and sour, the standard partner to thepla

ingredients.qty: 600g, boiled, peeled and broken into rough 3cm pieces

ingredients.note: use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
the Gujarati sweetness — not optional here

prepNotes: Boil the potatoes the night before if you can. Cold boiled potatoes break into rough pieces rather than turning to paste.
Break the potatoes with your hands, not a knife. Torn faces soak up gravy.
This shaak carries a deliberate hing note. Half a teaspoon reads as a lot but it is what the dish tastes of.

steps.text: Heat the oil and crackle the mustard seeds until they stop popping, then add the cumin.
Add the asafoetida, curry leaves and slit green chillies and let them sputter for 10 seconds.
steps.tip: Have the pan lid within reach — wet curry leaves spit hard.

steps.text: Stir in the turmeric, chilli powder and coriander powder off the direct flame for 5 seconds so they bloom without burning.
Add the chopped tomato and cook 5-6 minutes over medium heat until it collapses and the oil shows at the edges.
Tip in the broken potatoes and salt and turn them gently until yellow all over.
Pour in the water, bring to a simmer, cover and cook 8 minutes on low.
Uncover, add the jaggery and mash a few pieces of potato against the side of the pan to thicken the gravy.
steps.tip: Mashing three or four pieces is what turns thin liquid into a gravy that coats. No cornflour needed.

steps.text: Simmer uncovered 3-4 minutes more until it is loose but clinging, then take off the heat.
Stir in the lemon juice and coriander and check the balance — it should read salty first, then sweet, then sour.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. It thickens as it sits; reheat with a splash of water over low heat and re-check the lemon, which fades overnight.

recipes.name: Bhinda Sambhariya
recipes.subtitle: whole okra stuffed with a peanut, coconut and sesame masala, cooked gently in a covered pan

ingredients.qty: 3 tbsp, dry-roasted until it smells nutty

ingredients.note: use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Wash the okra a good hour ahead and dry each pod completely with a cloth. Any water left on them turns the whole dish slimy.
Roast the peanuts, sesame and besan separately and let them cool before grinding — warm nuts go pasty.
Choose small pods, 7-8cm; large okra is fibrous and splits when stuffed.

steps.text: Top and tail the okra and slit each pod lengthways down one side, stopping short of both ends so it stays whole.
Mix the ground peanut, roasted besan, sesame, coconut, all the ground spices, sugar, salt, ginger, chilli, coriander leaves and lemon juice into a crumbly stuffing.
steps.tip: It should just clump when squeezed. If it is dust-dry, add a teaspoon of oil, not water.

steps.text: Press the stuffing into each pod with a small spoon or your fingertip, filling but not splitting them.
Heat the oil in a wide kadhai, pop the mustard seeds and add the asafoetida.
Lay the stuffed okra in a single layer and let them sit undisturbed 4 minutes to blister on the underside.
steps.tip: Stirring early breaks the pods open and spills the masala.

steps.text: Turn each pod gently with tongs, cover, and cook on low heat 12 minutes.
Uncover, shake the pan and cook 5 minutes more until the okra is tender, the surfaces are lightly browned and no sliminess remains.
steps.tip: If it still looks ropey, finish uncovered on higher heat for 2 minutes — dry heat fixes it.

steps.text: Scatter over any leftover stuffing, let it toast for a minute, and serve with rotli.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat uncovered in a dry pan so the okra crisps again rather than steaming; the microwave makes it slippery.

recipes.name: Dal Dhokli
recipes.subtitle: spiced wheat diamonds simmered soft in sweet-sour toor dal, a one-pot supper

ingredients.note: for the dhokli dough

prepNotes: Soak the toor dal 30 minutes and the peanuts along with it.
Make the dhokli dough first and let it rest 20 minutes while the dal cooks; rested dough rolls thin without springing back.
Keep 300ml of hot water aside. The dhokli drink a startling amount of liquid as they cook and again as they sit.

steps.text: Pressure cook the drained dal with the peanuts, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 800ml water for 4 whistles, then let the pressure drop naturally.
Meanwhile knead the atta, besan, ajwain, remaining turmeric, 1/2 tsp chilli powder, salt and 2 tbsp oil with about 70ml water into a stiff dough. Cover and rest 20 minutes.
steps.tip: Stiffer than roti dough — soft dhokli disintegrate in the dal.

steps.text: Whisk the cooked dal smooth, add the remaining water, tamarind, jaggery, ginger, green chilli, remaining chilli powder and salt, and bring to a simmer.
Roll the dough very thin, 2mm, and cut into 4cm diamonds.
steps.tip: Thin is the whole point. Thick dhokli stay doughy in the middle.

steps.text: Bring the dal to a rolling boil and drop the diamonds in a few at a time, stirring gently between additions.
steps.tip: Add them one by one and keep the dal moving or they weld into a clump.

steps.text: Simmer uncovered 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the dhokli are cooked through and the dal has thickened around them.
Heat the ghee, pop the mustard and cumin seeds with the cinnamon, cloves and dried chilli.
Add the curry leaves and asafoetida, then pour the tempering over the pot.
Simmer 3 minutes more, thinning with hot water to a thick soup.
Scatter the coriander over and serve in bowls with a spoon of ghee and raw chopped onion on the side.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately. It keeps 2 days refrigerated but thickens to a paste; reheat with a lot of hot water and expect the dhokli to be softer the next day.

recipes.name: Doodhpak
recipes.subtitle: rice simmered down slowly in milk until thick, scented with saffron and cardamom

ingredients.note: full-fat only; skimmed milk will not thicken

ingredients.qty: a generous pinch, soaked in 2 tbsp warm milk

prepNotes: Soak the rice 30 minutes, then drain and crush it lightly between your palms so a few grains break — the broken starch is what thickens doodhpak.
Rub the base of the heavy pan with ghee before the milk goes in. It is the simplest insurance against catching.
Steep the saffron in warm milk for at least 10 minutes so it gives up its colour.

steps.text: Grease a heavy-bottomed pan with the ghee and bring the milk to a boil over medium heat, stirring so it does not catch.
Add the drained rice and lower the heat to a bare simmer.
Cook uncovered for 40-45 minutes, stirring every 4-5 minutes and scraping the base and sides each time.
steps.tip: Scrape the sides back in as the milk skins. Those scrapings are what give doodhpak its grainy richness.

steps.text: When the milk has reduced by about a third and coats the back of a spoon, the rice should be completely soft and starting to break.
Add the sugar and stir 5 minutes. The mixture will loosen noticeably before it thickens again.
steps.tip: Sugar always goes in after the rice is soft. Added early, the grains stay firm no matter how long you cook.

steps.text: Stir in the saffron milk and the ground cardamom and simmer 5 minutes more.
Add the slivered almonds and cook a final 3 minutes. It should be pourable but leave a clear trail behind the spoon.
steps.tip: Stop while it still looks slightly loose — doodhpak thickens a great deal as it cools.

steps.text: Take off the heat, grate over a scraping of nutmeg and scatter the pistachios.
Cool to room temperature, then chill at least 3 hours. Serve cold with hot puri.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated in a covered container. It sets firm when cold; loosen with 2-3 tbsp of cold milk and stir well before serving rather than reheating.

recipes.name: Dudhi na Muthiya
recipes.subtitle: steamed bottle-gourd and flour rolls, sliced and crisped in a sesame tempering

ingredients.note: keeps the crumb open rather than pasty

ingredients.qty: 6 tbsp — 3 into the dough, 3 for the tempering

prepNotes: Grate the dudhi and leave it in a bowl for 10 minutes, then squeeze it lightly and keep the juice — that liquid is all the water the dough needs.
Do not add plain water to the dough. If it is too stiff, add the reserved dudhi juice a spoon at a time.
The steamed rolls must cool completely before slicing, or they crumble. Steam them an hour ahead if you can.

steps.text: Mix the grated dudhi with the atta, besan, rava, ginger, green chilli, turmeric, chilli powder, coriander powder, sugar, salt, lemon juice, baking soda and 3 tbsp oil.
Bring it together into a soft dough using only the reserved dudhi juice. It should be softer than chapati dough but hold a shape.
steps.tip: Work it quickly and lightly — a kneaded, over-worked muthiya dough steams up dense.

steps.text: Oil your palms and roll the dough into 3 logs about 5cm thick. Set them on a greased steamer plate.
Steam over boiling water for 22-25 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean and the surface is matte, not tacky.
Cool completely, at least 30 minutes, then cut into 1.5cm slices.
steps.tip: Slicing warm is the single most common failure. Wait.

steps.text: Heat the remaining 3 tbsp oil in a kadhai, crackle the mustard seeds, then add the sesame, asafoetida and curry leaves.
Lay the slices in and fry over medium heat, turning once, 4-5 minutes a side until the edges are golden and crisp.
steps.tip: Turn them once only and with a flat spatula; they break if you toss them.

steps.text: Scatter with coriander and coconut and serve hot with chai or plain yogurt.

recipes.storage: Steamed logs keep 3 days refrigerated, unsliced and wrapped. Slice and temper fresh — muthiya reheated after tempering goes soft and oily.

recipes.name: Fafda
recipes.subtitle: crisp-chewy strips of fried gram flour dough, the classic sunday breakfast

ingredients.qty: 250g, coarse ground if you can get it

ingredients.note: standing in for papad khar, the traditional alkaline salt

ingredients.qty: 3 tbsp for the dough, plus 1 litre for frying

ingredients.note: fried alongside and salted, the classic accompaniment

prepNotes: Dissolve the baking soda and salt in the warm water before it touches the flour, so the alkali is evenly distributed.
The dough needs 20 minutes covered rest; it becomes stretchy and stops tearing under the palm.
Clear a long stretch of oiled worktop or the back of a steel tray — fafda is pressed out, not rolled, and needs room.

steps.text: Mix the besan, ajwain, black pepper and turmeric in a wide bowl.
Rub in the 3 tbsp oil until the mixture holds its shape when squeezed.
Add the soda-and-salt water gradually and knead 8 minutes into a smooth, firm, elastic dough.
steps.tip: Knead it properly. Underworked dough gives brittle fafda instead of the signature chew.

steps.text: Cover and rest 20 minutes.
Pinch off a walnut-sized piece, place it on an oiled surface, and press it away from you with the heel of your palm into a long strip about 12cm by 3cm.
steps.tip: One firm continuous push. Repeated pressing makes ragged, uneven strips.

steps.text: Lift the strip with a flat scraper and lay it on an oiled tray while you press the rest.
Heat the frying oil to 175C — a scrap of dough should rise steadily, not violently.
steps.tip: Too hot and the fafda browns before it dries; too cool and it drinks oil.

steps.text: Slide in 3-4 strips at a time and fry 2-3 minutes, turning once, until pale gold and no longer bubbling hard.
Drain on a rack, not paper, so both faces stay crisp.
Fry the slit green chillies for 30 seconds, salt them, and serve alongside with kadhi or papaya sambharo.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days in an airtight tin at room temperature and stays crisp. Do not refrigerate — the damp turns it leathery. Refresh in a 150C oven for 5 minutes.

recipes.name: Gujarati Dal
recipes.subtitle: thin toor dal balanced sweet with jaggery and sharp with tamarind

ingredients.note: cooked in with the dal until soft
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the toor dal 30 minutes; it cooks more evenly and the peanuts soften alongside it.
Soak the tamarind in 4 tbsp hot water for 15 minutes and squeeze out the pulp, or use ready-made concentrate at half the quantity.
This dal is meant to be drinkably thin — thinner than any north Indian dal. Keep hot water at hand to loosen it.

steps.text: Pressure cook the drained dal with the peanuts, turmeric and 700ml water for 4 whistles, then let the pressure drop naturally.
steps.tip: The peanuts must go in from the start; added later they stay hard.

steps.text: Whisk the cooked dal smooth and thin it with the remaining water until it pours easily from a ladle.
Add the tamarind pulp, jaggery, tomato, ginger, green chilli and salt and simmer 12 minutes.
Taste and adjust — it should read sweet, then sour, then salty, with heat arriving last.
steps.tip: Balance it while it is thin; a thick dal tastes sweeter than it is and misleads you.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a small pan and pop the mustard seeds.
Add the cumin, fenugreek, cinnamon, cloves and dried red chilli and let them darken 15 seconds.
Add the curry leaves, chilli powder and asafoetida off the heat, then pour the whole tempering into the dal.
steps.tip: Off the heat for the chilli powder, or it turns black and bitter.

steps.text: Simmer 3 minutes more, scatter the coriander over and serve with rice and a spoon of ghee.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and tastes better on day two. Reheat with plenty of extra water — it thickens considerably in the fridge.

recipes.name: Gujarati Kadhi
recipes.subtitle: thin sweet-sour yogurt and gram flour soup, drunk as much as eaten

ingredients.note: day-old yogurt gives the right tang
sifted, or it will lump
Gujarati kadhi is sweeter than most
a scant pinch — more turns it bitter
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
to finish

prepNotes: Take the yogurt out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead — fridge-cold yogurt splits the moment it meets heat.
Whisk the besan into the yogurt first, before any water goes in, and keep whisking until no grains remain.
Crush the ginger and chilli together in a mortar rather than chopping; kadhi wants their juice, not pieces.

steps.text: Whisk the besan into the yogurt until completely smooth, then thin it with the water a little at a time.
steps.tip: Lumps at this stage never dissolve later — they cook into rubbery specks.

steps.text: Stir in the turmeric, jaggery, ginger, green chilli and salt, and set the pan over medium heat.
Bring it to a boil stirring constantly in one direction, about 8 minutes. It will foam up as it reaches the boil.
steps.tip: Do not walk away or stop stirring before the first boil — that is exactly when it curdles.

steps.text: Drop the heat and simmer 10 minutes, until the raw besan smell is gone and the kadhi coats a spoon thinly.
Heat the ghee in a small pan and add the mustard seeds; wait for them to pop.
Add the cumin, fenugreek, cloves, cinnamon and dried red chilli, and let them darken for 15 seconds.
steps.tip: Fenugreek burns in seconds and turns the whole pot bitter — pull the pan the moment it colours.

steps.text: Add the curry leaves and asafoetida, stand back from the spatter, and pour the tempering straight into the kadhi.
Simmer 2 minutes more, scatter the coriander over and serve hot with plain rice or khichdi.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat gently over low heat with a splash of water, stirring — a hard boil on reheating will split it.

recipes.name: Gujarati Khichdi
recipes.subtitle: soft rice and moong dal cooked to a porridge, eaten with kadhi and ghee

ingredients.note: four parts liquid to one of grain, by volume
half in the pot, half poured over at the table
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Rinse the rice and dal together in three changes of water until it runs clear, then soak 20 minutes and drain.
This khichdi is deliberately soft and loose — the grains should surrender, not stay separate. Do not cut the water.
Have the kadhi made and hot before the khichdi is done; khichdi stiffens fast as it sits.

steps.text: Heat half the ghee in the pressure cooker and crackle the cumin seeds until they turn a shade darker.
Add the asafoetida, ginger and green chilli and let them sizzle 10 seconds.
Tip in the drained rice and dal and stir 2 minutes until every grain is glossed with ghee.
steps.tip: This brief fry keeps the khichdi from turning to glue.

steps.text: Add the water, turmeric and salt and stir well, scraping the base.
Close the cooker and cook for 4 whistles on medium heat, then let the pressure fall on its own.
Open, whisk briefly and thin with hot water if it has set firm — it should slump off a spoon.
steps.tip: Only hot water. Cold water added to hot khichdi makes it gluey.

steps.text: Crack the black pepper over, pour the remaining ghee on top and serve with kadhi.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. It sets solid when cold; reheat in a pan with a generous splash of hot water, breaking it up with a spoon.

recipes.name: Guvar nu Shaak
recipes.subtitle: cluster beans cooked down with crushed peanut and sesame until the bitterness turns nutty

ingredients.note: pick young, flexible pods; woody ones stay bitter
guvar is heavy; ajwain settles it
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: String the beans properly: snap the tip and pull the fibre down each side. A single missed string ruins a mouthful.
Roast and crush the peanuts yourself and keep them coarse — powder disappears, coarse crush gives the dish its grain.
If the guvar is older and stringy, soak the cut pieces in warm salted water for 15 minutes before cooking.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai and crackle the mustard seeds, then add the ajwain and asafoetida.
Add the crushed garlic and green chilli and fry 1 minute until the garlic smells sweet.
Tip in the cut guvar and turn it through the oil for 3-4 minutes until the pods turn a brighter green.
Add the turmeric, chilli powder, coriander powder and salt and stir 30 seconds.
Pour in the water, cover and cook on low for 15 minutes, stirring twice.
steps.tip: Low and covered. Guvar cooked hard on high stays squeaky in the middle however long you leave it.

steps.text: Check a pod — it should be tender enough to crush between finger and thumb with no snap. Give it 5 minutes more if not.
Uncover, add the crushed peanut, sesame and jaggery and cook 4-5 minutes until the water has gone and the beans are coated in a dry, nutty masala.
steps.tip: Add the peanuts late. Boiled peanuts go soft and lose the whole point of them.

steps.text: Take off the heat, stir in the lemon juice and coriander, and serve with rotli and dal-bhaat.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. Reheat in a dry pan over medium heat, no water — this shaak is meant to be dry and water makes it sludgy.

recipes.name: Handvo
recipes.subtitle: savoury fermented rice and lentil cake with a crisp sesame crust

ingredients.note: short or medium grain
feeds the ferment
squeeze out and reserve the juice
added at the last second, for lift
most of it goes on top
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the rice, all three dals and the fenugreek together in plenty of water for 5 hours, then drain and grind coarse — handvo wants grit, not a smooth idli batter.
The ground batter needs 8-10 hours of fermentation, overnight in a warm spot. It should rise slightly and smell pleasantly sour.
Grate the bottle gourd only when you are ready to mix, and fold it in just before cooking; it weeps and thins the batter if it sits.

steps.text: Grind the soaked, drained rice and dals with the yogurt to a coarse batter, thick enough to drop off the spoon in a lump.
steps.tip: Add the reserved bottle gourd juice rather than water if you need to loosen it.

steps.text: Cover and leave in a warm place 8-10 hours to ferment.
Fold in the grated bottle gourd, ginger, chilli, turmeric, chilli powder, sugar, salt and coriander.
Heat 3 tbsp oil in a heavy 22cm pan, crackle the mustard and cumin seeds, then add the curry leaves, dried chilli and asafoetida.
Stir most of this tempering into the batter, leaving a spoonful and its oil in the pan.
Beat in the eno, pour the batter into the pan, level it and scatter the remaining sesame over the top.
steps.tip: Once the eno goes in the batter must hit the pan within a minute or the lift is lost.

steps.text: Cover and cook on the lowest heat 25 minutes, until the top is set and a skewer comes out clean.
steps.tip: Low and slow. On high heat you get a burnt base over raw batter.

steps.text: Drizzle the remaining oil around the edge, flip the cake or slide it under a hot grill, and cook 10 minutes more until the crust is deep brown and crisp.
Rest 10 minutes in the pan before cutting into squares.
steps.tip: Cutting hot handvo tears it; the crumb needs to firm up.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. Reheat slices in a dry pan or a 180C oven for 8 minutes to bring the crust back; the microwave makes it soggy.

recipes.name: Khaman
recipes.subtitle: soft steamed gram-flour squares soaked in a sweet mustard-seed tempering

ingredients.note: coarse besan gives a better crumb than fine

ingredients.qty: 160ml for the batter, plus 120ml for the tempering
5 tbsp — 1 into the batter, 4 into the tempering water
4 — 2 ground into the batter, 2 slit for the tempering

ingredients.note: just for colour, no more
the only lift there is — add last

ingredients.qty: 5 tbsp — 2 into the batter, 3 for the tempering

ingredients.note: use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Grease a 20cm tin and get the steamer water to a rolling boil before you mix the batter. Once eno goes in the batter will not wait.
Grind the ginger with 2 of the green chillies into a coarse paste; the other 2 chillies stay whole for the tempering.
Rest the batter 15 minutes so the besan hydrates — this is what stops the khaman tasting raw.

steps.text: Whisk the besan with 160ml water, 1 tbsp sugar, the ginger-chilli paste, turmeric, salt, 2 tbsp oil and the lemon juice into a smooth batter the thickness of pancake batter. Rest 15 minutes.
steps.tip: Whisk in one direction and break every lump now — you cannot fix them later.

steps.text: Bring the steamer to a hard boil and oil the tin.
Stir the eno into the batter with a teaspoon of water, whisk hard for 10 seconds until it froths and doubles, and pour straight into the tin.
steps.tip: Do not beat it down after it froths. Pour and steam immediately.

steps.text: Steam covered on high for 15-18 minutes, until a skewer pushed into the centre comes out clean and the top springs back.
Lift out, rest 5 minutes, then cut into 4cm diamonds and loosen them in the tin.
Heat the remaining 3 tbsp oil, crackle the mustard seeds, then add the sesame, asafoetida, curry leaves and slit chillies. Stand back — the leaves spit.
Pour in 120ml water and 4 tbsp sugar, bring to a boil and cook 1 minute until the sugar dissolves.
steps.tip: This watery syrup looks wrong. It is right — it is what makes khaman moist rather than dry.

steps.text: Spoon the hot tempering evenly over the cut khaman, tipping the tin so it reaches the corners. Leave 10 minutes to drink it in.
Scatter with coriander and grated coconut and serve warm with green chutney.

recipes.storage: Best the day it is made. Keeps 2 days covered in the fridge; steam the pieces 3-4 minutes to bring the sponge back, never microwave them dry.

recipes.name: Khaman Dhokla
recipes.subtitle: Steamed, aerated gram flour squares with a sweet-sour mustard tempering

ingredients.note: optional, for structure; omit to keep it gluten-free
omit to keep it vegan; use 2 tbsp extra water
added last, off the heat

prepNotes: Everything must be ready before the Eno goes in. It starts releasing gas immediately and the batter has to reach the steam within about thirty seconds or the dhokla will be dense.
Have the steamer already at a rolling boil and the tin greased before you begin mixing.
The tempering is poured over the cooked dhokla with a little water in it. That water is what keeps the squares moist.

steps.text: Set a steamer to boil and grease a shallow tin. Whisk the besan, rava, yogurt, turmeric, ginger, chilli, salt, 1 tbsp oil and about 3/4 cup water into a smooth, thick-but-pourable batter. Rest 10 minutes.
Stir in the juice of half a lemon. Add the Eno, whisk briskly for 20 seconds as it foams and visibly lightens, and pour immediately into the tin.
steps.tip: Do not beat it after this point; you will knock the air back out.

steps.text: Steam covered on high for 15-18 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean and the surface springs back. Cool 10 minutes, then cut into squares.
For the tempering, heat the remaining oil, splutter the mustard seeds, add the sesame, curry leaves, asafoetida and any remaining slit chillies.
Take the pan off the heat and carefully add 1/3 cup water, the sugar and the remaining lemon juice. Return to the heat and simmer just until the sugar dissolves.
Spoon the warm tempering evenly over the dhokla and leave it 15 minutes to soak in fully. Scatter with coriander before serving.

recipes.storage: Best the day it is made. Keeps 2 days refrigerated in a sealed box; revive by steaming 3-4 minutes, which restores the softness. Do not microwave uncovered, it goes rubbery.

recipes.name: Khandvi
recipes.subtitle: silky gram flour sheets rolled tight and dressed with mustard seeds and coconut

ingredients.note: or 150g sour yogurt whisked with 350ml water

ingredients.qty: 4 — two as paste for the batter, two slit for the tempering

ingredients.note: use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Oil two large flat trays or the back of two baking sheets and have them within arm's reach before you start cooking. The batter sets as it cools and will not wait.
Sift the besan twice and whisk the batter until glassy-smooth — a single lump becomes a hole in the sheet.
The buttermilk must be sour. Fresh, sweet buttermilk gives a flat-tasting khandvi.

steps.text: Whisk the besan, buttermilk, turmeric, ginger, chilli paste, asafoetida and salt to a completely smooth, lump-free batter.
steps.tip: Strain it through a sieve if you have any doubt at all.

steps.text: Pour into a heavy pan and cook over medium heat, stirring without pause with a flat spatula.
steps.tip: Constant stirring, scraping the base and corners — the moment you stop it catches and lumps.

steps.text: After 10-12 minutes it will thicken to a glossy paste that pulls away from the sides of the pan.
Test it: spread a teaspoon on an oiled tray, wait 30 seconds and try to peel it up. If it lifts clean, it is ready; if it smears, cook 2 minutes more and test again.
steps.tip: This test is the whole recipe. Undercooked batter will never roll.

steps.text: Working fast, pour the batter onto the oiled trays and spread it paper-thin with a flat scraper.
Let it cool 5 minutes until set and no longer tacky, then cut into strips about 6cm wide.
Roll each strip up tightly from one end and stand the rolls on a serving plate.
Heat the oil, pop the mustard seeds, add the sesame, slit chillies, curry leaves and a pinch of asafoetida, and pour it over the rolls.
Scatter the coconut and coriander over and serve at room temperature.

recipes.storage: Best the day it is made. Keeps 2 days refrigerated but firms up; bring back to room temperature for an hour before serving. Do not reheat.

recipes.name: Khichu
recipes.subtitle: scalded rice-flour dough spiked with green chilli and cumin, eaten hot with a pool of oil

ingredients.note: fine rice flour, not the coarse idli variety
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
stands in for papad khar; gives the springy chew

ingredients.qty: 4 tbsp, to pour over at the table

prepNotes: Measure the flour before you boil the water — the flour goes in all at once and there is no time to weigh mid-way.
Use a heavy pan. Khichu catches and scorches in a thin one within seconds.
Khichu is eaten straight from the pan while it steams. Have everyone at the table before you start.

steps.text: Bring the water, salt, cumin seeds, chopped green chilli, asafoetida and baking soda to a rolling boil in a heavy pan.
steps.tip: Taste the water now. It should be a shade saltier than you want the finished khichu.

steps.text: Turn the heat to low and tip in all the rice flour at once. Do not stir yet.
Cover and leave 2 minutes so the flour steams through.
Now beat hard with a wooden spoon until it comes together into a single lump with no dry pockets, about 2 minutes.
steps.tip: Keep it on the heat while you beat — off the heat it goes gluey.

steps.text: Cover again and steam on the lowest heat for 6-8 minutes, stirring once, until the dough looks glossy and pulls away from the sides.
Wet your palm with cold water and knead the hot dough in the pan for a minute until smooth and elastic.
steps.tip: Wet hands, not oiled — water is what keeps it from sticking and lets you work it hot.

steps.text: Pinch off portions, shape into rough rounds and press a dimple into each with your thumb.
Pour a spoonful of oil into every dimple, dust with chilli powder and sesame, and eat immediately with the oil running.

recipes.storage: Khichu does not keep well as a soft dough. Refrigerate leftovers up to 2 days, then roll thin, dry in the sun and fry as papad — which is what the dough was invented for.

recipes.name: Lasaniya Batata
recipes.subtitle: baby potatoes crushed and simmered in a fierce red garlic masala

ingredients.note: small ones, roughly equal in size

ingredients.qty: 20 cloves, crushed to a coarse paste

ingredients.note: for the red colour without the burn
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
thickens the masala and gives it body

prepNotes: Boil the potatoes ahead: 3 whistles in a pressure cooker or 15 minutes in salted water, until a knife slides in with slight resistance. They finish cooking in the masala.
Crush rather than slice the boiled potatoes — press each one with your palm until it splits. The rough surfaces hold masala the way a cut face never will.
Mix the ground spices into 4 tbsp water to a paste before they go in the pan; dry powder scorches in hot oil in seconds.

steps.text: Boil the baby potatoes until just tender, drain and cool 10 minutes.
Press each potato with the flat of your palm until the skin splits and it flattens slightly. Leave the skins on.
steps.tip: Split, not mashed. You want craggy edges, not puree.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai, crackle the cumin seeds, add the asafoetida and the crushed garlic.
Fry the garlic over medium-low heat for 3-4 minutes until it turns pale gold and the raw edge goes.
steps.tip: Pale gold only. Browned garlic turns the whole dish bitter and there is a lot of it here.

steps.text: Stir in the spice paste and the ground sesame and cook 2 minutes until the oil rises red around the edges.
Add the crushed potatoes and slit green chillies and turn them through the masala until every piece is coated.
Pour in the water, season with salt, cover and simmer on low for 10-12 minutes, shaking the pan occasionally.
Uncover and cook 4-5 minutes more until the gravy clings thickly to the potatoes and pools of red oil sit on top.
steps.tip: That surfacing oil is the finish line. Stop before it and the masala tastes raw.

steps.text: Finish with lemon juice and coriander and serve with bajra rotlo or plain khichdi.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and tastes better on day two. Reheat in a pan with 2 tbsp water over low heat; the potatoes turn mealy in a microwave.

recipes.name: Mag ni Dal
recipes.subtitle: loose split yellow moong finished with a ghee and cumin tempering, the plainest weekday dal

ingredients.qty: 200g, rinsed until the water runs clear

ingredients.note: use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Rinse the moong dal in three changes of water. The starch you wash off is what makes an unrinsed dal taste cloudy.
Soak 20 minutes if you are cooking in an open pan; skip the soak in a pressure cooker.
Salt goes in after the dal is soft, not before — early salt keeps split moong from breaking down.

steps.text: Put the rinsed dal, water and turmeric in a pressure cooker and cook 3 whistles, then let the pressure drop naturally. In an open pan, simmer 30-35 minutes topping up water.
Open up and whisk the dal briefly — it should be loose enough to pour, like thin cream. Add hot water if it has tightened.
steps.tip: Mag ni dal is meant to be thin. If a spoon stands up in it you have gone too far.

steps.text: Stir in salt, the grated ginger and the slit green chillies and simmer 5 minutes.
Heat the ghee in a small pan until it shimmers, then add the cumin seeds and let them turn a shade darker and smell toasted.
Add the broken dried chillies, curry leaves and asafoetida and pull the pan off the heat after 5 seconds.
steps.tip: Five seconds. Asafoetida burns almost instantly and turns acrid.

steps.text: Pour the tempering into the dal — it should hiss — and clap the lid on for a minute to trap the aroma.
Stir in the lemon juice and cracked pepper off the heat.
steps.tip: Lemon after the heat is off. Boiled lemon juice goes bitter.

steps.text: Scatter with coriander and serve over plain rice with a spoon of extra ghee.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and thickens considerably. Loosen with hot water when reheating and add a fresh squeeze of lemon; the tempering aroma does not survive a second day.

recipes.name: Methi Muthiya
recipes.subtitle: steamed fenugreek dumplings squeezed by hand, then tossed in a sesame tempering

ingredients.note: for a coarser, more traditional crumb
keeps them light

prepNotes: Salt the chopped methi and rest it 10 minutes, then squeeze hard. The water it gives up is usually enough to bind the dough with no extra liquid.
Oil the steamer plate well and oil your palms before shaping, or the dough sticks to everything.
Muthiya must cool completely before slicing, so build in 20 minutes of waiting before the tempering stage.

steps.text: Mix the flours, sesame, ajwain, ground spices, sugar, salt, ginger, chilli and lemon juice in a bowl.
Add the squeezed methi and 2 tbsp of the oil and work it into a stiff dough, using the methi water only if needed.
steps.tip: Keep it firm. Slack dough collapses in the steamer.

steps.text: Work in the baking soda, then divide the dough into four and roll each into a log about 4cm thick, squeezing it in your fist so it keeps the finger marks that give muthiya its name.
Steam the logs 20 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean and the surface is dry.
Cool completely, at least 20 minutes, then cut into 2cm slices.
steps.tip: Slicing warm muthiya tears it into crumbs.

steps.text: Heat the remaining oil in a kadhai, pop the mustard seeds, and add the curry leaves and asafoetida.
Add the slices and pan-fry 6-8 minutes, turning occasionally, until the cut faces are golden and crisp.
steps.tip: Turn rarely, not constantly — each face needs contact time to colour.

steps.text: Scatter the coconut and coriander over and serve hot with tea or masala chai.

recipes.storage: Steamed logs keep 4 days refrigerated. Slice and fry to order; fried muthiya keeps 2 days and crisps up again in a hot dry pan.

recipes.name: Methi Thepla
recipes.subtitle: soft fenugreek-flecked flatbreads that travel for days without going stale

ingredients.note: keeps them soft and adds body
the softening agent — do not skip

ingredients.qty: 2 tbsp for the dough, plus more for roasting

ingredients.note: oil if you want them to keep longer

prepNotes: Wash the methi and dry it thoroughly on a cloth. Wet leaves make a slack dough that needs extra flour and turns the theplas tough.
Salt the chopped methi and leave it 10 minutes, then squeeze — it releases water and loses its raw bitterness.
The dough must rest at least 20 minutes; unrested thepla dough fights the rolling pin and shrinks back.

steps.text: Mix the atta, besan, chopped methi, all the spices, sesame and salt in a wide bowl.
Rub in the 2 tbsp oil until the flour looks like damp sand, then add the yogurt, ginger and chilli.
Bring it together with water added a spoonful at a time into a soft, pliable dough — softer than roti dough.
steps.tip: Methi keeps releasing water as it sits, so start drier than you think you need.

steps.text: Cover and rest the dough 20 minutes.
Divide into 12 balls and roll each to a thin round about 15cm across, dusting lightly with atta.
Cook on a hot tawa 40 seconds, until small bubbles rise, then flip.
Smear ghee on the cooked side, flip again, and press the edges down with a cloth so it puffs and browns in spots.
steps.tip: Brown freckles, not a uniform tan — an over-cooked thepla goes brittle and will not roll.

steps.text: Stack the cooked theplas in a cloth-lined box so they steam each other soft.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4-5 days in an airtight box at room temperature, a week refrigerated. Eat at room temperature with chundo or plain yogurt; no reheating needed.

recipes.name: Patra
recipes.subtitle: colocasia leaves layered with spiced tamarind gram paste, steamed then crisped

ingredients.note: the big heart-shaped arbi leaves, not the root
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
to finish

prepNotes: Wash the leaves and wipe them completely dry, then shave down the thick central vein with a knife so each leaf lies flat.
The tamarind is not optional flavouring — its acid is what neutralises the itch in colocasia leaves. Keep the paste properly sour and taste it before spreading.
Roll the bundles at least 30 minutes before steaming, or make them a day ahead and refrigerate; they slice far more neatly when firm.

steps.text: Whisk the besan with the tamarind pulp, jaggery, ginger, chilli, all the ground spices, ajwain, asafoetida and salt, adding water slowly to a thick spreadable paste.
steps.tip: It should be the consistency of soft butter — runny paste slides out of the roll while steaming.

steps.text: Taste the paste. It should be aggressively sweet-sour and salty; the leaves dilute it a great deal.
Lay a leaf vein-side up, spread a thin even layer of paste over it, and place a second leaf on top pointing the other way.
Build stacks of three or four leaves, pasting between each.
Fold the two long sides inward, spread paste on the fold, then roll up tightly from the base into a firm log.
steps.tip: Tight rolls hold their spiral. A loose roll unravels in the steamer.

steps.text: Steam the logs 30 minutes, until a skewer slides in without resistance and the outside is dull and dry to the touch.
Cool completely, then cut into 1.5cm slices.
steps.tip: Slicing while warm squashes the spiral flat — wait for it to firm up.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai, pop the mustard seeds with the sesame, and lay the slices in a single layer.
Shallow-fry 3 minutes a side until the edges are crisp and browned.
Scatter the coconut and coriander over and serve warm with tea.

recipes.storage: Steamed unfried logs keep 4 days refrigerated and freeze for a month. Slice and fry to order; already-fried patra goes soft and is best refreshed in a hot dry pan.

recipes.name: Ringan no Olo
recipes.subtitle: fire-roasted aubergine mashed with raw garlic and green chilli, smoky and fierce

ingredients.note: the fat purple globe kind, not slim ones

ingredients.qty: 12 cloves, crushed to a coarse paste
ingredients.note: olo is a garlic dish; do not cut this back
generous oil is what makes it olo and not bharta
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Rub the whole aubergines with a little oil and slit each one twice so steam escapes — otherwise they burst on the flame.
Roast directly on a gas flame if you have one. That char is the entire flavour of the dish and an oven does not give it.
Half the garlic goes in raw at the end. Crush it to a paste rather than chopping so it disappears into the mash.

steps.text: Set the aubergines straight on a medium gas flame, turning every couple of minutes, 12-15 minutes in all, until the skin is blistered black all over and the flesh has collapsed.
steps.tip: Push a knife into the thickest part. If there is any resistance, keep roasting — undercooked olo tastes bitter.

steps.text: Rest them in a covered bowl 5 minutes, then peel off the charred skin and mash the flesh coarsely with a fork. Leave some texture.
Heat the oil in a kadhai, crackle the cumin, add the asafoetida and half the crushed garlic and fry 30 seconds until it smells sweet, not brown.
Add the onion and cook over medium heat until soft and pale gold, about 6 minutes.
Stir in half the green chilli, the turmeric, chilli powder and coriander powder, then the tomato. Cook 6-7 minutes until the tomato breaks down and the oil separates at the edges.
steps.tip: Wait for the oil to separate. That is the point at which the masala stops tasting of raw spice.

steps.text: Fold in the mashed aubergine and salt. Cook uncovered 8 minutes, mashing against the side of the pan, until it thickens and darkens.
Take it off the heat and stir through the remaining raw crushed garlic, the remaining green chilli and the lemon juice.
steps.tip: The raw garlic at the end is what makes it Kathiawadi. Add it off the heat so it stays sharp.

steps.text: Rest 5 minutes, stir in the coriander and serve with hot bajra rotlo and a spoon of butter or a raw onion.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated and the smoke deepens overnight. Reheat in a pan with a teaspoon of oil; do not add water, it goes watery and flat.

recipes.name: Sev Tameta nu Shaak
recipes.subtitle: soupy sweet-sharp tomato curry finished with crisp gram flour sev

ingredients.qty: 100g, pressed through a sev maker and fried
ingredients.note: or simply use 100g ready-made nylon sev
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
kashmiri for colour without heat

prepNotes: Use properly ripe tomatoes; the gravy has nothing else to hide behind.
Keep the sev in a sealed box until the moment you serve. It goes limp within two minutes of hitting the gravy, which is the point, but only on the plate.
Make the gravy slightly thinner and sweeter than you would eat it plain — the sev soaks up liquid and mutes it.

steps.text: Heat the oil and pop the mustard seeds, then add the cumin, curry leaves and asafoetida.
Add the onion and garlic and fry 5 minutes until the onion is soft and translucent, not browned.
Stir in the turmeric, chilli powder and coriander powder off the heat for 10 seconds so they bloom without burning.
steps.tip: Ground spices scorch in hot dry oil in under a minute — the tomatoes should follow immediately.

steps.text: Tip in the tomatoes, green chilli and salt and cook 8 minutes, pressing them down, until they collapse and the oil beads at the edges.
Add the jaggery and the water and simmer 6 minutes into a loose, pourable gravy.
steps.tip: It should be soupier than a normal shaak — thin it further if in doubt.

steps.text: Taste and balance: it wants to land sweet first, then sour, then hot.
Ladle into bowls, pile the sev over the top and scatter the coriander.
Serve at once with rotli or bhakri, while the sev is still crunchy.

recipes.storage: The gravy keeps 3 days refrigerated and reheats well with a splash of water. Never store it with the sev in — add that fresh each time.

recipes.name: Shrikhand
recipes.subtitle: hung yogurt whipped with sugar, saffron and cardamom into a thick tart cream

ingredients.note: hung overnight to about 450g of chakka
adjust to how sour the yogurt is
to bloom the saffron

prepNotes: Hang the yogurt in a double layer of muslin over a bowl in the fridge for 8 hours or overnight. You want about 450g of firm chakka left behind.
Do not throw the drained whey away — it makes excellent dough water for thepla or rotli.
Warm the milk and steep the saffron in it for 15 minutes; saffron dropped in dry gives colour but no perfume.

steps.text: Crush the saffron between your fingers into the warm milk and leave it to steep 15 minutes until the milk is deep orange.
Tip the hung yogurt into a bowl and add the sugar.
Beat with a whisk for 4-5 minutes until the sugar has fully dissolved and the mixture is glossy and smooth.
steps.tip: Rub a little between your fingers — any grittiness means it needs more whisking, not more time in the fridge.

steps.text: Pass it through a fine sieve, pressing with a spatula, for a properly silken texture.
steps.tip: This sieving step is what separates good shrikhand from grainy shrikhand.

steps.text: Fold in the saffron milk, ground cardamom and nutmeg.
Taste and adjust the sugar; it should be tart first and sweet second.
Chill at least 3 hours, until set firm enough to hold a peak.
steps.tip: Serve properly cold. Lukewarm shrikhand tastes cloying.

steps.text: Spoon into bowls, scatter the pistachios and almonds over and serve with hot puris.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated in a sealed box. Do not freeze — it separates on thawing. Stir before serving if any whey has pooled.

recipes.name: Sukhdi
recipes.subtitle: wheat flour toasted in ghee and set with jaggery, crumbly and warming

ingredients.note: sukhdi is a ghee sweet; less ghee gives a sandy, dry set
the traditional warming note, especially in winter

prepNotes: Grease a 20cm tray or thali before you start. Once the jaggery goes in you have about 40 seconds to spread it.
Grate the jaggery finely and have it weighed and beside the pan. Lumps will not melt in time.
Work over low heat throughout. Sukhdi is a slow toast, not a fry.

steps.text: Melt the ghee in a heavy kadhai over low heat.
Add the atta and stir continuously with a flat spatula, keeping the flour moving across the base.
Roast 12-15 minutes over low heat until the flour turns the colour of wet sand and smells like biscuits.
steps.tip: Colour is not the reliable cue — smell is. When the raw floury smell is replaced by a toasted, nutty one, it is done.

steps.text: Stir in the dry ginger powder and cardamom and cook 20 seconds.
Take the pan completely off the heat and let it stand 60 seconds to cool slightly.
steps.tip: This pause matters. Jaggery added to a screaming-hot pan turns to hard caramel and the sukhdi sets like glass.

steps.text: Add all the jaggery at once and stir hard until it melts into the flour and the mixture turns glossy and pourable, about 45 seconds.
Tip immediately into the greased tray and level the top with the back of a greased steel bowl.
Score into diamonds while still hot, after about 3 minutes, then leave to set completely for 30 minutes.
steps.tip: Score hot, break cold. Cutting a fully set sukhdi shatters it.

steps.text: Break along the score lines and serve at room temperature.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 weeks in an airtight tin at room temperature and does not need refrigeration. If it hardens in cold weather, warm a piece for 10 seconds before eating.

recipes.name: Undhiyu
recipes.subtitle: Surat's winter casserole of root vegetables and methi dumplings, cooked upside down

ingredients.note: for the muthiya dumplings

prepNotes: Undhiyu takes its name from undhu, upside down: it was buried in an inverted earthen pot and cooked in a pit. The domestic version layers everything in a heavy pot and never stirs it.
The green masala of coconut, coriander, chilli and ginger goes both inside the slit vegetables and between the layers. Make it first.

steps.text: Blend the coconut, coriander, green chilli, ginger, sesame, peanut, jaggery, lemon and salt to a coarse green masala.
Make muthiya: knead the besan with chopped methi, a spoon of the masala, ajwain and a little water into a stiff dough; shape small dumplings and shallow fry until golden. Set aside.
Stuff the slit eggplants and any halved potatoes with the green masala.
In a heavy pot, heat the oil with asafoetida, then layer the vegetables hardest-first: yam and sweet potato at the bottom, then banana and potato, then beans and peas, stuffed eggplant on top.
steps.tip: Layer by cooking time and do not stir — that is the whole method.

steps.text: Spoon over the remaining masala and a splash of water, cover tightly and cook on low heat 35-40 minutes.
Add the muthiya for the last 10 minutes so they soften without dissolving. Fold once, very gently, at the end.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat gently and briefly; the vegetables are already soft and will collapse. Not suitable for freezing.

recipes.name: Vagharelo Bhaat
recipes.subtitle: yesterday's rice fried up with mustard seeds, potato and peas into a proper meal

ingredients.note: day-old rice from the fridge, grains separate
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Use cold rice straight from the fridge. Fresh warm rice turns to paste the moment it hits the pan.
Break up any clumps with wet fingers before you start, so you are not doing it in a hot pan.
Dice the potato small — 1cm — or it will still be raw when the rice is hot.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai and crackle the mustard seeds, then add the cumin, asafoetida, curry leaves and slit chillies.
Add the onion and cook 4 minutes over medium-high heat until the edges colour.
Add the diced potato, turn to coat, cover and cook 6-7 minutes until a piece gives easily to a fork.
steps.tip: Cover the pan for this. The potato steams tender rather than frying dry and hard.

steps.text: Stir in the peas, turmeric and chilli powder and cook 2 minutes.
Add the cold rice, salt and sugar and fold gently with a flat spatula until every grain is yellow.
steps.tip: Fold, do not stir. A spoon stirred in circles smashes the grains.

steps.text: Raise the heat and leave the rice undisturbed for 2 minutes so the bottom layer catches slightly, then fold once.
Cook 2 minutes more until the rice is hot all the way through and smells toasted.
Off the heat, stir in the lemon juice and coriander and serve with plain yogurt or chaas.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat covered in a pan with 1 tbsp water over medium heat; the microwave dries the grains at the edges.

recipes.name: Aloo ke Gutke
recipes.subtitle: kumaoni boiled potatoes tossed hot in mustard oil, whole chillies and coriander seed

ingredients.qty: 600g, boiled, peeled and cut into 2cm chunks

ingredients.note: stands in for jakhya, the wild hill seed used at home
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Boil the potatoes the day before if you can and refrigerate them. Cold cooked potato holds its shape in the pan instead of mashing.
Break the potatoes into chunks with your hands rather than cutting them. The ragged surfaces catch far more spice.
Have every spice measured out beside the stove — the tempering here takes under a minute from start to finish.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes, then drop the heat to medium and wait 30 seconds.
Add the cumin and mustard seeds together. They should pop within 5 seconds.
Throw in the broken red chillies and the hing and stir for 15 seconds until the chillies darken a shade.
steps.tip: The chillies scorch fast. Move straight to the next step the moment they change colour.

steps.text: Add the turmeric, coriander powder and chilli powder, stir once, and immediately tip in the potatoes.
Toss over medium-high heat for 6-8 minutes until the potatoes are patched with gold and crusty at the edges.
steps.tip: Resist stirring constantly. Let them sit still for a minute at a time to build a crust.

steps.text: Add the salt, dry ginger powder, amchur and slit green chillies. Toss for 2 more minutes.
Kill the heat, fold through the coriander leaves and serve hot with plain rice or with a bowl of dal.

recipes.storage: Best within a couple of hours. Keeps 2 days refrigerated; revive in a dry pan over high heat rather than the microwave, which leaves them soggy.

recipes.name: Arsa
recipes.subtitle: deep-fried rice flour and jaggery cakes, crisp at the rim and chewy in the middle

ingredients.note: hill cooks soak and grind their own rice; coarse shop flour works
mustard oil is traditional if you want the sharper hill version

prepNotes: The dough must rest overnight at room temperature, covered. This is not optional — the rest is what gives arsa its chew, and same-day dough fries hard and flat.
If you are grinding your own, soak the rice 6 hours, drain, dry in the shade for 2 hours until just damp, then grind coarse and sieve.
Have a bowl of cold water beside you for wetting your palms while shaping. The dough is very sticky.

steps.text: Melt the jaggery with 120ml water over low heat, stirring, until it dissolves, then strain out the grit through a fine sieve.
Return the syrup to the pan and boil until it reaches one-thread consistency — a drop lifted between finger and thumb pulls a single strand, about 6 minutes.
steps.tip: This is the make-or-break step. Under-cooked syrup gives soggy arsa; taken too far it sets hard and the dough will not come together.

steps.text: Pour the hot syrup over the rice flour in a wide bowl, add the sesame, fennel, cardamom and salt, and mix with a wooden spoon.
Once it is cool enough to handle, knead 4-5 minutes into a soft, sticky dough that just holds together.
Cover and rest at room temperature overnight, 8-10 hours.
Next day, wet your palms and shape walnut-sized pieces into flat discs about 6cm across and 1cm thick.
steps.tip: Keep re-wetting your hands. Dry palms tear the discs apart.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai to medium-low, about 160C — a scrap of dough should rise slowly after 4 seconds.
steps.tip: Hot oil browns the outside while the centre stays raw. Low and slow is the whole technique.

steps.text: Slide in 3-4 discs at a time and fry 6-8 minutes, spooning hot oil over them and turning once, until deep reddish brown.
Lift onto a rack and press each one gently with a slotted spoon to squeeze out oil. Cool completely before eating — they firm up as they sit.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 weeks in an airtight tin at room temperature, which is why arsa is made in batches for weddings and Diwali. Do not refrigerate; it goes hard and loses the chew.

recipes.name: Auriya Kaddu
recipes.subtitle: pumpkin in a sharp ground-mustard and yogurt gravy, the tangy course of a dham

ingredients.qty: 2 tbsp, soaked 2 hours and ground to a paste
ingredients.note: the auriya — this ground mustard is the whole dish
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
balances the bite of the mustard

prepNotes: Soak the mustard seeds 2 hours, then grind with 2 tbsp of the soaking water to a fine grey paste. Ground dry, they stay gritty and turn bitter.
Take the yogurt out of the fridge an hour ahead. Cold yogurt splits the moment it meets a hot pan.
Whisk the yogurt with the turmeric and chilli powder before it goes anywhere near the heat.

steps.text: Heat the ghee and mustard oil together until the mustard oil stops smelling raw, about 1 minute.
Crackle the fenugreek seeds and broken red chillies for 20 seconds, then add the hing.
steps.tip: Fenugreek goes from fragrant to bitter in about 10 seconds. Pull it the moment it turns reddish-brown.

steps.text: Add the pumpkin cubes and toss over medium heat 5 minutes until the edges catch a little colour.
Take the pan off the heat for a minute so it cools, then pour in the whisked spiced yogurt and stir continuously.
steps.tip: Off the heat and stirring — this is the only reliable way to stop the yogurt curdling.

steps.text: Return to a low flame and cook, stirring in one direction, until the yogurt loses its raw smell and thickens slightly, about 4 minutes.
Stir in the ground mustard paste, 200ml water and salt. Simmer uncovered 12 minutes until the pumpkin is tender at a knifepoint but not falling apart.
steps.tip: Never boil the mustard hard — heat turns it acrid. A bare simmer only.

steps.text: Add the amchur and sugar, cook 2 minutes more and taste. It should be sour, mustardy and only faintly sweet.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat and serve with rice as part of a dham.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat over the lowest flame with a spoon of water — a hard reheat splits the yogurt and sharpens the mustard.

recipes.name: Babru
recipes.subtitle: shimla-style fried breads packed with spiced ground urad dal, crisp outside and savoury through

ingredients.note: a little refined flour keeps the shell crisp rather than chewy

prepNotes: Soak the urad dal 4 hours, then drain it hard in a sieve for 10 minutes. Wet dal makes a sloppy filling that tears the dough.
The dough needs 30 minutes rest before rolling, so make it first and the filling while it sits.
Grind the dal coarse, not smooth - babru filling should be grainy.

steps.text: Mix the atta, maida, 1 tsp salt and the mustard oil, then add water gradually to a firm, smooth dough. Knead 6 minutes.
Cover and rest 30 minutes. The dough should press back slowly when poked.
Grind the drained urad dal with the green chillies and ginger to a coarse, dry paste, using at most 2 tbsp water.
steps.tip: If it looks like batter you have gone too far. Stop while you can still see broken grains.

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp of the frying oil in a pan, crackle the cumin, ajwain and asafoetida, then add the dal paste.
Cook the dal on medium for 8 to 10 minutes, breaking up lumps, until it dries out and comes away from the pan in a single crumbly mass.
steps.tip: Filling that is still moist will steam inside the babru and burst it open in the oil.

steps.text: Stir in the coriander powder, chilli powder, amchur, crushed fennel, garam masala, salt and coriander leaves. Cook 2 minutes, then cool completely.
Divide the dough into 10 balls. Flatten each in your palm, cup it, put in a heaped tablespoon of cold filling, gather the edges over the top and pinch shut. Press flat.
Roll each stuffed ball gently to about 10cm across, working from the centre out with light pressure.
steps.tip: Press hard and the filling pushes through. If a tear opens, patch it with a scrap of dough.

steps.text: Heat the oil to 175C. Slide in two babrus at a time and press the centre lightly with a slotted spoon so they puff.
Fry 2 minutes a side until deep golden and blistered. Drain and serve hot with kaddu ka khatta or a tamarind chutney.

recipes.storage: Eat within a couple of hours while the shell is crisp. They keep a day in an airtight tin and revive in a 180C oven for 5 minutes; refrigeration makes them leathery.

recipes.name: Bhatt Ki Churkani
recipes.subtitle: kumaoni black beans roasted in mustard oil and simmered into a dark, smoky, rice-thickened gravy

ingredients.note: stands in for bhatt, the small Kumaoni black soybean; use bhatt if you can find it and skip the soaking in favour of a dry roast
the traditional thickener - churkani means the gravy, not the bean
compounded-free hing, both for the gluten and because jambu is hard to source outside the hills

prepNotes: Soak the beans overnight. If you have actual bhatt, dry roast them in a heavy pan for 5 minutes until they crackle and smell toasted, then cook them unsoaked.
Whisk the rice flour into 150ml cold water and leave it aside. Added dry to a hot pan it lumps immediately.
This is a mustard oil dish through and through - a neutral oil version tastes of nothing much.

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp mustard oil in a heavy pan until it smokes, then cool it 20 seconds. Add the drained beans and roast them on medium for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring, until the skins wrinkle and blister.
steps.tip: This roast is where the smokiness comes from. Take it to the point where the pan smells nutty, just short of burnt.

steps.text: Transfer the beans to a pressure cooker with 800ml water and 1 tsp salt. Cook for 6 whistles and let the pressure fall naturally.
Heat the remaining 2 tbsp mustard oil in a kadhai to smoking, then cool briefly. Crackle the cumin and fenugreek seeds and the broken red chillies, 20 seconds.
steps.tip: Fenugreek goes bitter fast. Pull it off the heat the moment it browns.

steps.text: Add the asafoetida, then the crushed garlic, and fry 1 minute to pale gold.
Stir in the ginger and green chillies, then the turmeric, coriander powder and chilli powder. Fry 30 seconds.
Tip in the cooked beans with all their liquid and bring to a boil.
Stir the rice flour slurry once more and pour it in slowly while stirring hard. The gravy will thicken visibly within a minute.
steps.tip: Pour in a thin stream and keep the spoon moving, or you will be picking out lumps for the next ten minutes.

steps.text: Simmer uncovered on low for 15 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes, until the gravy turns glossy and dark and coats a spoon thickly.
Check the salt, scatter over the coriander leaves and serve with plain rice and a spoon of raw mustard oil on top if you like it sharp.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and sets almost solid as it cools. Reheat on low with 100ml water, whisking to bring the thickened gravy back together.

recipes.name: Chainsoo
recipes.subtitle: garhwali black gram roasted and ground dry, then cooked to a smoky near-black mash

ingredients.note: the black skin is what gives chainsoo its colour
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Do not soak the dal. Chainsoo starts with dry roasting, and damp dal will steam in the pan instead of toasting.
Grind the roasted dal coarsely, to the texture of fine semolina rather than flour. Ground too fine it goes gluey.
Traditionally this is cooked in an iron kadhai, which is part of where the colour comes from. Use the heaviest pan you own.

steps.text: Dry roast the whole urad in a heavy kadhai over medium heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring constantly, until it smells nutty and a few grains crack.
steps.tip: Roast until dark and fragrant but never smoking. Scorched dal makes the whole pot bitter.

steps.text: Cool completely on a plate, then grind to a coarse meal.
steps.tip: Grinding hot dal releases oil and clumps the grinder. Give it 15 minutes.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil until it smokes, cut the heat for a minute, then crackle the cumin and red chillies.
Add the hing, garlic and ginger, and fry 90 seconds until the garlic turns pale gold.
Stir in the ground dal and roast it in the oil over low heat for 5 minutes, stirring the whole time. It will darken and smell toasty.
steps.tip: This second roast in oil is what separates chainsoo from ordinary dal. Keep the heat low and keep moving.

steps.text: Add the turmeric, coriander powder and chilli powder and fry 1 minute.
Pour in the hot water a ladle at a time, whisking after each addition so no lumps form.
steps.tip: Hot water, added gradually. Cold water straight in sets the ground dal into lumps you cannot break.

steps.text: Add salt and simmer uncovered on a low flame for 25 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until it is thick, glossy and almost black.
Stir in the garam masala, rest 5 minutes off the heat, scatter coriander and serve with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. It sets very firm — reheat with a good half cup of water, whisking until it loosens back to a pouring mash.

recipes.name: Chana Dal Dham
recipes.subtitle: sweet-sour chana dal from the dham feast, no onion or garlic anywhere in it

ingredients.note: the botis of Himachal cook dham entirely in ghee
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
saunth, the dham cook's stand-in for fresh ginger
extra sourness if the tamarind is mild

prepNotes: Soak the chana dal 3 hours. Unsoaked dal will not soften evenly and dham dal must hold its shape, not collapse.
Soak 20g tamarind in 100ml hot water for 20 minutes, then squeeze and strain to get the 2 tbsp of pulp.
Dham is cooked without onion or garlic by tradition, so all the depth has to come from the ghee, the hing and the long tempering. Do not shortcut those.

steps.text: Pressure cook the drained dal with 750ml water, the turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 2 whistles, then lower the flame and give it 6 minutes more.
steps.tip: You want grains that yield when pressed but still look like grains.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a heavy pan until it thins and shimmers, then add the cumin. It should crackle within 3 seconds.
Drop in the hing and count to five. It will foam and smell nutty, not acrid.
steps.tip: If it darkens past pale gold the whole pot turns bitter. Pull the pan off the heat if it moves fast.

steps.text: Stir in the coriander powder, chilli powder and dry ginger powder off the heat for 20 seconds so they bloom without burning.
Pour in the cooked dal with its liquid and bring to a simmer, 5 minutes.
Add the tamarind pulp and the jaggery and simmer uncovered 15 minutes, stirring now and then, until the gravy coats the back of a spoon.
steps.tip: Taste at 10 minutes. It should land sour first, sweet second — add jaggery a teaspoon at a time.

steps.text: Crush in the anardana and the garam masala, simmer 3 minutes more, then check the salt.
Rest the pot off the heat for 10 minutes before serving. Scatter the coriander leaves and serve with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and tastes better on day two. Reheat gently with 3-4 tbsp water — it thickens hard as it cools.

recipes.name: Chana Madra
recipes.subtitle: chickpeas simmered slowly in whisked yogurt until the gravy is silky, faintly sour and heavy with whole spice

ingredients.note: sour, day-old curd is better than fresh
madra is a generous dish; do not cut this below 4 tbsp
stabilises the yogurt so it will not split
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
sonth carries the warmth that ginger root would in a plains curry
colour without heat
the Chamba touch, a sweet note against the sour curd

prepNotes: Soak the chickpeas overnight in plenty of water. They should more than double.
Take the yogurt out of the fridge an hour ahead. Cold yogurt splits the moment it meets hot ghee.
Whisk the yogurt with the besan and a pinch of salt until there is not a single lump, then keep the whisk in the bowl - you will use it again.

steps.text: Pressure cook the drained chickpeas with 500ml water and 1 tsp salt for 4 whistles, then let the pressure drop by itself. They should crush easily between finger and thumb but still hold their shape.
steps.tip: Undercooked chana will never soften later - the acid in the yogurt sets them hard.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a heavy kadhai until it thins and shimmers. Add the cumin, cinnamon, black cardamom, green cardamom, cloves and bay leaves and let them swell and crackle, about 40 seconds.
Add the asafoetida, count to five, then take the pan off the heat entirely and let it cool for a full minute.
steps.tip: This off-heat pause is the whole trick of madra. Yogurt going into ripping-hot ghee will curdle every time.

steps.text: Pour in the whisked yogurt, return to the lowest possible flame and stir continuously in one direction for 8 to 10 minutes, until the yogurt loses its raw smell and thickens to the consistency of pouring cream.
steps.tip: Do not stop stirring and do not cover the pan until the yogurt has come to a boil once.

steps.text: Stir in the coriander powder, fennel powder, dry ginger, turmeric and kashmiri chilli. Cook 3 minutes more - the gravy will turn glossy and the ghee will start to bead at the edges.
Add the drained chickpeas along with 150ml of their cooking water. Season with salt.
Simmer uncovered on low for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the gravy coats the back of a spoon and a clear rim of ghee sits around the edge of the pan.
steps.tip: That ring of separated ghee is how Chamba cooks judge madra is done.

steps.text: Fold in the almonds and raisins and cook 3 minutes so the raisins plump.
Finish with the garam masala, cover and rest off the heat for 10 minutes before serving with plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and genuinely improves on day two. Reheat very gently on low with a splash of water - a hard boil will break the yogurt.

recipes.name: Gahat ki Dal
recipes.subtitle: kumaoni horse gram simmered long and dark, earthy and warming for a cold night

ingredients.note: gahat or kulth — the hill winter pulse
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
the traditional thickener if the dal stays thin

prepNotes: Soak the horse gram overnight, at least 10 hours. It is the hardest pulse in an Indian kitchen and nothing shortens that.
Discard the soaking water and rinse twice — it carries most of what makes gahat heavy to digest.
In the hills the leftover cooking liquid is drunk on its own as a peppery broth, so keep it thin enough to pour.

steps.text: Pressure cook the drained horse gram with 1.2 litres water, the turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles, then simmer on low pressure 15 minutes.
steps.tip: Fewer than 6 whistles and the grains stay stubbornly hard in the middle.

steps.text: Let the pressure fall by itself, then check: a grain should crush easily between finger and thumb. If not, give it 3 more whistles.
Heat the mustard oil in a separate pan until it smokes, cut the heat for a minute, then crackle the cumin and red chillies.
Add the hing, then the crushed garlic and ginger, and fry 90 seconds until the garlic is pale gold and smells sweet.
steps.tip: Garlic browner than pale gold turns the dal bitter over the long simmer.

steps.text: Add the onion and cook 7 minutes to a soft light brown, then the tomato and cook 4 minutes until it collapses.
Stir in the coriander powder and chilli powder and fry 1 minute until the oil separates at the edges.
Tip the whole tempering into the cooked dal, stir well and simmer uncovered 20 minutes so the flavours settle in.
steps.tip: This uncovered simmer is where gahat gets its depth. Do not cut it short.
