steps.text: If it is still watery, stir in the rice flour slurry and cook 3 minutes until it just coats a spoon.
Check the salt, scatter coriander and serve with rice and a spoon of ghee if you are not keeping it vegan.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and freezes well for a month. Reheat with plenty of water — it sets almost solid when cold.

recipes.name: Kaapa
recipes.subtitle: garhwali spinach thickened with gram flour, garlicky and eaten by the bowl with rice

ingredients.note: the thickener — no cream or dairy goes into kaapa
whole seeds, not kasuri methi
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Wash the spinach in three changes of water. Hill spinach comes in gritty and grit in kaapa is unforgiveable.
Whisk the besan into 200ml cold water until completely smooth before you start cooking, and leave it aside. Lumps will not come out later.
Blanch and blend the spinach only if you want it smooth; many Garhwali homes leave it coarse and chopped.

steps.text: Blanch the spinach in boiling water for 90 seconds, drain and plunge into cold water to fix the colour.
steps.tip: Ninety seconds, no more. Overcooked spinach goes olive and dull.

steps.text: Squeeze out the excess water and either chop it fine or pulse it briefly in a blender to a coarse puree.
Heat the mustard oil until it smokes, cut the flame for a minute, then crackle the cumin and fenugreek seeds for 20 seconds.
steps.tip: Fenugreek turns bitter quickly — the moment it reddens, move on.

steps.text: Add the hing, red chillies, garlic, ginger and green chillies and fry 2 minutes until the garlic is golden.
Stir in the turmeric and coriander powder, then pour in the smooth besan slurry, whisking continuously.
Cook the besan mixture on a low flame for 6-8 minutes until it thickens and stops smelling of raw flour.
steps.tip: Raw besan is the single most common fault in kaapa. Give it the full 8 minutes.

steps.text: Add the spinach, the remaining 200ml water and salt. Simmer uncovered 10 minutes until it is thick enough to hold a ridge from the spoon.
Finish with the lemon juice off the heat and serve with hot rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat gently with a splash of water; the colour dulls on day two but the flavour improves.

recipes.name: Kaddu Ka Khatta
recipes.subtitle: pumpkin cooked down with tamarind, pomegranate seed and jaggery into the sharp sour dish that cuts a dham

ingredients.qty: 700g, cut into 3cm cubes with the skin left on
ingredients.note: the skin keeps the pieces from disintegrating
heat it to smoking first to take off the raw pungency
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

ingredients.qty: 2 tbsp thick pulp, from a lime-sized ball soaked in hot water

ingredients.note: dried pomegranate seed, the sourness Himachal actually uses

prepNotes: Soak the tamarind in 100ml hot water for 20 minutes, then squeeze and strain out the pulp.
Grind the anardana coarsely in a mortar just before cooking - ready-ground powder goes flat within weeks.
Do not peel the pumpkin. The skin holds the cubes together through a long simmer.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes faintly and the sharp smell drops away, about 2 minutes. Take it off the heat for 20 seconds to cool slightly.
steps.tip: Raw mustard oil tastes acrid. Smoking it once is the whole difference.

steps.text: Add the fenugreek seeds and let them darken to a nut brown, no more than 15 seconds, then the cumin.
steps.tip: Fenugreek turns bitter the second it goes past brown - have the cumin in your hand ready.

steps.text: Stir in the asafoetida, then immediately add the turmeric, chilli powder, coriander powder and dry ginger. Fry 20 seconds.
Tip in the pumpkin and toss to coat every piece in the spiced oil. Fry on medium for 5 minutes until the edges start to catch.
Pour in 300ml water, add salt, cover and simmer 12 to 15 minutes until a knife slides into a cube with no resistance.
Add the tamarind pulp, the ground anardana and the jaggery. Stir gently - from here on you want the cubes intact.
Simmer uncovered 8 to 10 minutes, mashing four or five pieces against the side of the pan, until the gravy thickens to a loose chutney that clings to the pumpkin.
steps.tip: Taste now and balance: it should read sour first, sweet second, never cloying. More jaggery or more tamarind, a spoon at a time.

steps.text: Finish with garam masala and coriander leaves. Serve at room temperature alongside rice and madra.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and the sourness settles and deepens. Serve cold or at room temperature; it is not a dish that wants reheating, though a minute on low is fine.

recipes.name: Khatta Meat
recipes.subtitle: chamba mutton curry made sour with pomegranate seed and dried mango, thin and fiercely spiced

ingredients.note: shoulder and neck give the best gravy
the defining sourness — do not substitute lemon
rounds off the sourness without sweetening the curry

prepNotes: Bring the mutton to room temperature for 30 minutes before cooking. Cold meat straight from the fridge seizes in hot oil.
Grind the anardana coarsely in a dry grinder just before you cook. Pre-ground pomegranate seed goes flat and stale within weeks.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking point and let it cool for a minute before you start. Raw mustard oil is harsh and this curry has nowhere to hide it.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil until it smokes, cut the flame for 60 seconds, then return it to medium.
Crackle the cumin, black cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and bay leaf for 30 seconds until the cardamom smells smoky.
Add the sliced onion and fry 10-12 minutes to a deep even brown, stirring often.
steps.tip: Brown, not black. Burnt onion turns the whole curry bitter and there is no fixing it.

steps.text: Stir in the ginger and garlic pastes and fry 2 minutes until the raw smell lifts.
Add the mutton and brown it hard over high heat for 8 minutes, stirring so every piece takes colour.
steps.tip: Do this in two batches if your pan is crowded — steamed meat gives a pale, thin curry.

steps.text: Lower the heat, add the turmeric, coriander powder, chilli powder and salt, and fry 4 minutes until oil beads at the edges.
Pour in 600ml water, bring to a boil, then pressure cook 4 whistles and rest until the pressure drops on its own, about 20 minutes.
Open the cooker, stir in the ground anardana and the amchur, and simmer uncovered 12 minutes. The gravy stays deliberately thin.
steps.tip: Add the sour agents only now — cooking them under pressure makes them dull and slightly bitter.

steps.text: Add the jaggery and garam masala, simmer 3 minutes, taste for salt and sourness.
Rest 10 minutes off the heat, scatter the coriander and serve with steamed rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated, better on the second day once the anardana settles. Reheat over low heat with a splash of water; do not boil hard or the meat tightens.

recipes.name: Kullu Trout
recipes.subtitle: whole river trout crisped in mustard oil with ajwain and a hard squeeze of lemon

ingredients.qty: 2 whole trout, about 300g each, cleaned and slashed 3 times a side
ingredients.note: catalogued simply as fish — use trout, or any firm river fish
carom is the hill cook's fish spice; it cuts the oiliness
for colour without heat

ingredients.qty: 1, half juiced and half in wedges

ingredients.note: a light dusting for extra crust

prepNotes: Pat the fish bone dry inside and out with kitchen paper. Any surface water and the marinade slides off and the skin steams instead of crisping.
Marinate 20 minutes only. Lemon juice on a delicate river fish for longer than that starts to cure the flesh and it goes chalky.
Bring the fish to room temperature before it hits the pan.

steps.text: Mix the turmeric, kashmiri chilli, chilli powder, ajwain, black pepper, ginger, garlic, lemon juice and salt into a thick paste.
Rub the paste over the fish and well into the slashes and the cavity. Rest 20 minutes.
steps.tip: Push it into the cuts with your fingers — that is the only way seasoning reaches the flesh of a whole fish.

steps.text: Dust each fish lightly with rice flour on both sides and shake off the excess.
Heat the mustard oil on a heavy tawa until it smokes, then cut the heat to medium for a minute.
Lay the fish in away from you and fry undisturbed for 5 minutes.
steps.tip: Do not poke it. The skin releases from the pan by itself when the crust has formed.

steps.text: Turn once with a wide spatula and fry the second side 4-5 minutes until the thickest part flakes at a fork.
Lift onto a warm plate, rest 2 minutes, scatter coriander and serve with lemon wedges and hot rice.

recipes.storage: Best eaten within the hour — the crust softens fast. Leftovers keep 1 day refrigerated; flake the cold flesh into a salad rather than reheating.

recipes.name: Mash Ki Dal
recipes.subtitle: whole black urad cooked down thick and buttery over a mustard oil base, the everyday hill dal

ingredients.note: gives body and a little sweetness
stirred in at the end, not cooked in
compounded-free hing keeps this gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the urad and chana dal together for at least 6 hours. Unsoaked whole urad takes an hour of pressure and still eats chalky.
Chop the onion fine - in the hills this dal is not blended, so the onion has to melt into it.
Have the ghee at room temperature; it goes in off the heat at the end.

steps.text: Pressure cook the drained dals with 900ml water, the turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 5 whistles, then 15 minutes on the lowest flame. Let the pressure drop naturally.
steps.tip: The dal is ready when a grain smears to paste between your fingers with no grit at the centre.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes lightly, then cool it 20 seconds off the flame.
Crackle the cumin, add the asafoetida, then the garlic. Fry 40 seconds until it just turns pale gold.
steps.tip: Garlic past gold goes bitter and there is nothing in this dal to hide it behind.

steps.text: Add the onion and cook on medium, stirring, for 10 to 12 minutes until it is properly brown at the edges and sweet-smelling.
Stir in the ginger and green chillies, then the coriander powder, chilli powder and dry ginger. Fry 30 seconds.
Add the tomatoes and cook 6 to 8 minutes, pressing them down, until they break completely and the oil pulls away to the sides.
Pour the cooked dal into the masala. Simmer uncovered 15 to 20 minutes on low, stirring and mashing against the pan, until it thickens enough to hold a furrow behind the spoon.
steps.tip: This long open simmer is what separates hill mash dal from a thin plains dal. Do not shortcut it.

steps.text: Check the salt, sprinkle over the garam masala and take off the heat.
Stir in the raw ghee and the coriander leaves and cover for 5 minutes before serving with rice or a hot roti.
steps.tip: Adding the ghee off the heat keeps its aroma; cooked in, it just disappears.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and thickens to a paste. Loosen with hot water and reheat on low, then add a fresh half-spoon of ghee before serving.

recipes.name: Mittha
recipes.subtitle: saffron sweet rice studded with raisin, almond and apricot, the dish that closes every dham

ingredients.note: long grain matters here - the rice must stay separate

ingredients.qty: a generous pinch, soaked in 2 tbsp warm water

ingredients.note: the Lahaul touch; dried apricot is the fruit these valleys actually grow

prepNotes: Soak the rice 30 minutes, then drain it in a sieve for a full 10 minutes. Wet rice will clump and this dish lives on separate grains.
Steep the saffron in 2 tbsp of warm - not boiling - water for 15 minutes so it gives up all its colour.
Have the sugar weighed out. It goes in after the rice is nearly cooked, and by then there is no time to measure.

steps.text: Heat 4 tbsp of the ghee in a heavy pot. Fry the almonds until pale gold, about 90 seconds, then the raisins until they puff, 20 seconds. Lift both out and set aside.
steps.tip: Raisins burn in seconds and turn bitter. Watch them, do not walk away.

steps.text: Into the same ghee add the cardamom, cloves and cinnamon and let them sizzle for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the drained rice and fry gently for 3 minutes, turning with a flat spoon, until every grain is glossy and a few have turned opaque white.
steps.tip: Turn, do not stir. Broken grains go mushy later.

steps.text: Pour in 550ml water with the pinch of salt and half the saffron liquid. Bring to a hard boil.
Drop the heat to low, cover and cook 10 minutes until the water is absorbed and the rice is about three-quarters done - still firm at the core.
steps.tip: This stage is the one that decides the dish. Add sugar to fully cooked rice and it goes sticky; add it too early and the rice never softens.

steps.text: Sprinkle the sugar evenly over the surface, add the apricots, and do not stir. Cover and cook on the lowest heat 8 minutes - the sugar will melt and be drawn down through the rice.
Uncover, drizzle over the last tablespoon of ghee and the remaining saffron water, and fold through once with a fork.
Fold in the fried almonds, raisins and the coconut slivers. Cover and rest off the heat 10 minutes.
Fluff once more with a fork and serve warm, in small portions - it is richer than it looks.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated, where it will firm up. Reheat covered with 1 tbsp of water and a little ghee on low, or steam 5 minutes; it is also good cold.

recipes.name: Patrode
recipes.subtitle: colocasia leaves layered with spiced gram flour, steamed into rolls and fried in slices

ingredients.note: catalogued as colocasia — you want the leaves, arbi patta, not the corm
keeps the paste from going rubbery
the acid that neutralises the itch in the leaves
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
for the final tempering

prepNotes: Choose young colocasia leaves. Old ones carry far more calcium oxalate and will leave your throat scratching however much tamarind you use.
Shave the thick central rib flat with a knife on the underside of each leaf, or the rolls will not lie flat.
Soak 30g tamarind in 150ml hot water for 20 minutes and strain to get the 3 tbsp of pulp. Do not skip it — it is doing chemistry, not just flavour.
The steamed rolls must cool completely, ideally 2 hours or overnight, before you slice them. Warm rolls crumble.

steps.text: Wipe the leaves clean and shave down the raised central ribs so each leaf lies flat.

Whisk the besan, rice flour, tamarind pulp, jaggery, ajwain, turmeric, chilli powder, coriander powder, cumin powder, hing and salt with enough water to make a thick spreadable paste, about the consistency of peanut butter.
steps.tip: Too thin and it runs out of the rolls in the steamer. It should cling to a spoon turned sideways.

steps.text: Lay a leaf shiny side down, spread a thin even layer of paste over it, and lay a second leaf on top facing the opposite way. Build stacks of 4 leaves.
steps.tip: Thin layers. A thick smear steams into a wet, gummy centre.

steps.text: Fold the two long sides of each stack inward, spread a little more paste on the folds, then roll up tightly from the base into a firm log.
Steam the rolls seam side down for 25-30 minutes, until a knife pushed into the centre comes out clean.
Cool the rolls completely, at least 2 hours, then cut into 1.5cm thick slices.
steps.tip: Cold rolls cut cleanly. This is the difference between neat rounds and a broken mess.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes, cut the heat for a minute, then pop the mustard seeds and sesame.
Lay the slices in a single layer and shallow fry 3 minutes a side until crisp and browned at the edges.
Drain, scatter with coriander leaves and serve hot with tea, or with rice and dal as part of a meal.

recipes.storage: The steamed rolls keep 4 days refrigerated unsliced and freeze for a month — slice and fry straight from cold. Fried slices are best eaten the same day.

recipes.name: Rajma Madra
recipes.subtitle: red kidney beans in a thick soured-yogurt gravy, the dham version that eats richer than chana madra

ingredients.note: the small dark Chamba beans if you can get them
insurance against splitting
compounded-free hing keeps the dish gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the rajma at least 10 hours, ideally overnight. Beans that have not swollen to twice their size will not cook through.
Bring the yogurt to room temperature and whisk it with the besan until it pours like thin cream.
Have the whole spices measured into one small bowl - once the ghee is hot they all go in together.

steps.text: Pressure cook the drained rajma with 700ml fresh water and 1 tsp salt for 6 to 7 whistles, then let the pressure fall naturally. A bean should collapse when pressed, with the skin still intact.
steps.tip: Never add the yogurt to half-cooked beans. Acid stops rajma softening dead.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a heavy pan until it shimmers. Add cumin, black cardamom, green cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and bay leaves; they will foam and smell sweet within 30 to 40 seconds.
Add the asafoetida, then pull the pan off the flame and let it cool a full minute.
steps.tip: Hot ghee plus cold yogurt equals a grainy, broken gravy. The pause is not optional.

steps.text: Return the pan to the lowest heat and pour in the yogurt, stirring without pause for 8 to 10 minutes until it thickens and the raw sourness cooks off.
Stir in the coriander, fennel, dry ginger, turmeric and kashmiri chilli. Cook 3 minutes until the gravy turns a deep ochre and glossy.
Tip in the rajma with about 200ml of its cooking liquor and season with salt.
Crush a small ladleful of the beans against the side of the pan and stir back in - this thickens the gravy without flour.
steps.tip: Six or seven crushed beans is plenty; any more and you lose the texture.

steps.text: Simmer uncovered 25 minutes on low, stirring often, until the ghee separates and rises in a clear rim.
Sprinkle over the garam masala, cover and rest 10 minutes off the heat before serving with steamed rice.

recipes.storage: Refrigerates well for 3 days and thickens as it sits. Loosen with hot water and reheat on the lowest flame, stirring; do not let it boil hard or the yogurt will separate.

recipes.name: Sepu Vadi
recipes.subtitle: fried urad dal dumplings soaked soft in a spinach and yogurt gravy, the dish that marks a proper kangra dham

ingredients.note: thickens the gravy and holds the yogurt together
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the urad dal 5 hours. Drain it thoroughly - wet dal grinds into a batter that will not hold a shape.
Grind the dal with as little water as possible, then beat it by hand for 4 to 5 minutes until a spoonful floats in a glass of water. This aeration is what makes the vadis light.
Bring the yogurt to room temperature and whisk it with the besan so the gravy will not split.

steps.text: Grind the drained urad dal to a thick, coarse paste with the green chillies and grated ginger, using no more than 3 tbsp water.
steps.tip: Coarse, not silky. Sepu vadi should have a little bite left in it.

steps.text: Beat the paste vigorously for 4 to 5 minutes with salt until it lightens in colour and passes the float test.
Heat the frying oil to 170C. Drop in flat spoonfuls of the batter, four or five at a time, and fry 4 to 5 minutes until deep gold and firm. Drain on paper.
steps.tip: Too hot and the outside browns while the inside stays raw batter. A dropped bit should rise steadily, not violently.

steps.text: Cut each fried vadi in half through its thickness. This is what lets it drink up the gravy.
Boil the spinach in 200ml water for 4 minutes, then blend it to a smooth green puree with its liquid.
Heat the ghee in a kadhai, crackle the cumin, add the asafoetida and take the pan off the heat for a minute to cool.
On the lowest flame pour in the yogurt-besan mixture and stir continuously for 8 minutes until it thickens and stops smelling raw.
steps.tip: One direction, no stopping, low heat. If it splits there is no fixing it.

steps.text: Stir in the coriander powder, turmeric, kashmiri chilli, fennel and dry ginger, then the spinach puree and 200ml water. Season and simmer 8 minutes.
Slide in the halved vadis, cover and simmer very gently 10 minutes until they swell and turn spongy but still hold together.
steps.tip: Stir as little as possible now - a soaked vadi falls apart if you push it around.

steps.text: Finish with garam masala and coriander leaves and rest 5 minutes before serving with rice.

recipes.storage: Best the day it is made, while the vadis still have some structure. Keeps 2 days refrigerated; reheat covered on the lowest flame with a little water, without stirring.

recipes.name: Siddu
recipes.subtitle: steamed wheat buns risen slow and stuffed with crushed walnut and poppy seed, eaten swimming in ghee

ingredients.note: sours the dough and helps it rise; yeast is traditional in Kullu, this is the everyday shortcut
for serving, and this is not the place to be shy
the Kullu filling; the nuts should be gritty, not powdered

prepNotes: The dough needs 3 hours in a warm place. In a cold kitchen sit the covered bowl over a pan of hand-hot water.
Dry roast the poppy seeds in a pan until they smell nutty and start popping, about 2 minutes, then cool before crushing.
Crush the walnuts in a mortar or under a rolling pin. A blender turns them to oily paste.

steps.text: Mix the atta, baking soda and 1 tsp salt. Work in the yogurt, then the lukewarm water a little at a time, to a soft dough slightly stickier than roti dough. Knead 8 minutes.
steps.tip: Softer than you think is right. A stiff dough steams into a dense brick.

steps.text: Oil the surface, cover with a damp cloth and leave in a warm spot for 3 hours. It should look puffed and feel airy, not doubled like bread.
Meanwhile mix the crushed walnuts, roasted poppy seeds, mustard oil, green chilli, ginger, coriander leaves, ajwain, cumin powder, chilli powder, black pepper and salt into a damp, crumbly filling.
Knock the dough back gently and divide into 8 balls. Do not knead it hard again.
Roll each ball into a 12cm disc. Put 2 heaped tbsp of filling on one half, fold over into a half moon and press the curved edge firmly, then pleat it shut with your fingers.
steps.tip: Seal properly or the filling weeps out and the siddu collapses in the steamer.

steps.text: Rest the shaped siddus, covered, for 15 minutes while the steamer comes up to a rolling boil.
Grease the steamer plate, arrange the siddus with 2cm between them and steam on high for 18 to 20 minutes.
steps.tip: Do not lift the lid before 15 minutes - the drop in steam makes them sink.

steps.text: Test with a skewer through the thickest part: it should come out clean and dry. Give them 3 more minutes if not.
Take them out, split the tops slightly and pour a tablespoon of melted ghee over each. Serve hot with mash dal or a chutney.

recipes.storage: Best within a few hours. Keeps 2 days refrigerated; re-steam 6 to 8 minutes to bring back the softness, or slice and pan-fry in ghee. Do not microwave - they go rubbery.

recipes.name: Tudkiya Bhath
recipes.subtitle: chamba pahari rice cooked through with chana dal, potato and yogurt until every grain carries the masala
prepNotes: Soak the chana dal 2 hours and the rice 30 minutes, separately. They cook at very different speeds and the soaking is what brings them together.
Drain the rice in a sieve for 10 minutes before it goes in the pan so it fries rather than steams.
Whisk the yogurt to a pouring consistency and keep it out of the fridge.

steps.text: Heat the ghee and mustard oil together in a heavy pot until shimmering. Add the bay leaves, black cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and cumin and let them crackle for 30 seconds.
Add the sliced onion and fry on medium-high for 10 minutes until brown at the edges and shrunken to a third of its volume.
steps.tip: Real colour here is where the dish gets its depth. Pale onion gives a flat bhath.

steps.text: Stir in the garlic, ginger and green chillies and fry 1 minute until the raw smell goes.
Add the turmeric, coriander powder and kashmiri chilli, then the tomato. Cook 5 minutes until the tomato collapses and oil beads at the edge.
Take the pot off the heat for 30 seconds, then pour in the whisked yogurt on low and stir constantly for 4 minutes until it thickens and stops looking curdled.
steps.tip: Straight from fridge to hot pan is how this splits. Room temperature yogurt, low flame, keep stirring.

steps.text: Add the drained chana dal and potato cubes with 150ml water. Cover and simmer 10 minutes - the dal should be half done, still with a bite.
Fold in the drained rice as gently as you can and fry 2 minutes so each grain is coated.
Pour in 450ml hot water, add salt generously and the mint, and bring to a hard boil. Taste the water - it should be a shade saltier than you want the finished rice.
Cover tight, drop to the lowest flame and cook 12 minutes without lifting the lid.
Rest off the heat 10 minutes, then fork through with the garam masala and coriander leaves. Serve with plain yogurt.
steps.tip: Never stir with a spoon while it is hot - a fork lifted from the edge keeps the grains whole.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat covered with 2 tbsp of water sprinkled over, on low or in a steamer, so the grains soften rather than dry out.

recipes.name: Bagara Baingan
recipes.subtitle: small aubergines stewed whole in a sesame-peanut gravy sharp with tamarind

ingredients.qty: 8 small round ones, about 400g, stalks left on

prepNotes: Slit each aubergine into quarters from the base but leave the stalk end joined so it holds together, and drop them into salted water while you make the masala — this stops them browning.
Roast and cool the peanuts, sesame, coconut and poppy seeds before grinding; a warm paste splits when it hits the pan.
Soak the tamarind in hot water 20 minutes and strain.

steps.text: Dry-roast the peanuts 5 minutes until blistered, then rub off the skins. Roast the sesame, coconut and poppy seeds separately, each for about a minute, and cool everything.
Grind the roasted lot to a smooth paste with 120ml water.
steps.tip: A coarse paste gives a sandy gravy — keep grinding until it is genuinely smooth.

steps.text: Heat half the oil in a kadhai and fry the drained aubergines over medium heat for 6-7 minutes, turning, until the skins are blistered and the flesh has softened. Lift out.
steps.tip: Fry them before they go into the gravy; boiled aubergine collapses into mush.

steps.text: In the same oil fry the sliced onion until deep golden, about 10 minutes, then cool and grind to a paste.
Add the remaining oil, crackle the mustard, cumin and fenugreek, then add the curry leaves and green chillies.
Stir in the ginger and garlic pastes, cook 1 minute, then add the onion paste with the turmeric, chilli, coriander and cumin powders. Fry 3 minutes.
Add the ground nut-and-seed paste and cook on medium-low for 8 minutes until it thickens, darkens by a shade and oil beads at the edges.
Pour in the tamarind water and the rest of the water, season with salt and simmer 8 minutes until the gravy coats a spoon.
Lower the aubergines in, spoon gravy over them, cover and cook on low for 10 minutes until a knife slides through with no resistance.
steps.tip: Do not stir once they are in — tilt and swirl the pan instead.

steps.text: Rest off the heat for 10 minutes and finish with coriander leaves. Serve with bagara rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. Reheat covered over low heat with 2 tbsp water; microwaving tends to break the aubergines apart.

recipes.name: Bagara Khana
recipes.subtitle: everyday whole-spice rice, the plain partner to salan and dalcha

ingredients.note: or neutral oil
the smoky Deccani note; leave it out rather than substitute

prepNotes: Soak the rinsed rice for 30 minutes and drain it well for 10 minutes before cooking — wet rice steams unevenly.
Measure the water properly: 1.8 parts water to 1 part soaked rice by volume, and resist adding more mid-cook.
Have every whole spice out on a plate before you start; the tempering takes under a minute.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a heavy pot and add the cumin, bay leaf, cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, black cardamom, star anise and stone flower. Let them sizzle 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the curry leaves and sliced onion and fry 7-8 minutes until light golden and just beginning to crisp at the edges.
steps.tip: Light golden, not brown — this is bagara khana, not biryani; the rice should stay pale.

steps.text: Stir in the ginger and garlic pastes and the slit green chillies and cook 1 minute.
Add the drained rice and turn it gently through the ghee for 2 minutes until every grain is glossy.
steps.tip: Use a flat spatula and fold rather than stir — soaked grains snap easily.

steps.text: Pour in the water, add the salt and the mint, and bring to a full rolling boil.
Boil uncovered until the water level drops to the surface of the rice and craters appear, about 5 minutes.
Cover tightly, drop the heat to the lowest setting and cook 10 minutes without lifting the lid.
steps.tip: Every peek costs steam. Trust the timing.

steps.text: Rest off the heat, still covered, for 10 minutes, then fluff with a fork from the edges inwards and serve.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat by sprinkling over 2 tbsp water and steaming covered for 5 minutes, or microwaving under a damp cloth; dry reheating turns the grains hard.

recipes.name: Baghara Tamatar
recipes.subtitle: whole tomatoes simmered in the peanut, sesame and coconut gravy of the salan family

ingredients.qty: 500g small firm tomatoes, left whole and pricked twice each
small lump, soaked in 100ml hot water

ingredients.note: a salan gravy needs the oil; it separates out and is spooned off at the end

prepNotes: Choose small, firm tomatoes and prick each one twice with a fork so the gravy gets inside without the skin bursting.
Soak the tamarind in hot water for 15 minutes and strain before you start cooking.
Roast the peanuts, sesame and coconut separately, not together — they brown at completely different speeds.

steps.text: Dry-roast the peanuts over medium heat 5 minutes, until the skins blister. Cool and rub off most of the skins.
Toast the sesame 2 minutes until it pops, then the coconut 1 minute until golden. Cool everything.
Fry the sliced onion in 2 tbsp of the oil until golden, 10 minutes, then cool.
Grind the peanuts, sesame, coconut and fried onion with 150ml water to a smooth, thick paste.
steps.tip: Grind this longer than feels necessary. Gritty paste makes a gravy that never comes together.

steps.text: Heat the remaining oil in a kadhai and pop the mustard seeds, cumin, nigella and fenugreek, 20 seconds. Add the curry leaves and green chillies.
Add the ginger and garlic pastes and fry 1 minute, then the whole tomatoes, and roll them in the oil for 3 minutes.
Lift the tomatoes out and set aside. Add the ground paste with the chilli powder, turmeric and coriander powder, and fry over medium heat 8 minutes.
steps.tip: The paste catches easily. Stir every 30 seconds and scrape the base; you are waiting for the oil to rise to the surface.

steps.text: Pour in the strained tamarind water and 250ml plain water, add the salt and jaggery, and bring to a simmer.
Return the tomatoes, cover, and simmer on low 12 minutes, spooning gravy over them twice, until they are soft but still whole.
steps.tip: Do not stir hard once the tomatoes are back in, or they collapse into the gravy.

steps.text: Uncover and simmer 5 minutes more, until a slick of red oil separates on top. Scatter the coriander and rest 10 minutes before serving with bagara rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and improves overnight as the tomatoes take up the gravy. Reheat gently on the stovetop without stirring much; freeze up to 2 months.

recipes.name: Dalcha
recipes.subtitle: mutton and chana dal simmered with bottle gourd and a firm sour edge

ingredients.note: neck and rib pieces give the best body

prepNotes: Soak the chana dal for 30 minutes so it cooks at roughly the same rate as the mutton.
Soak the tamarind in hot water for 20 minutes, then squeeze and strain — dalcha is defined by its sourness, so do not skimp.
Cut the bottle gourd last; it goes in late and should not sit and weep.

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp oil in the pressure cooker and brown the sliced onion for 8 minutes until golden at the edges.
Add the ginger and garlic pastes and fry 1 minute, then the mutton. Sear on high for 5 minutes until the pieces lose their raw pink.
steps.tip: Sear in one layer; crowded meat steams and stays grey.

steps.text: Stir in the turmeric, chilli powder, coriander powder and salt, add the tomatoes, and cook 5 minutes until the tomatoes break down.
Add the drained chana dal and 1 litre of water. Pressure cook 4 whistles, about 20 minutes, then let the pressure drop naturally.
steps.tip: Natural release keeps the mutton tender; a forced release toughens it.

steps.text: Open, add the bottle gourd and the remaining water, and simmer uncovered 12 minutes until the gourd is translucent and yields to a spoon.
Pour in the tamarind water and the garam masala. Simmer 10 minutes more, mashing some of the dal against the side of the pot to thicken it.
steps.tip: Add tamarind only after the dal is soft — acid early keeps pulses hard.

steps.text: Taste for salt and sour; the balance should make you sit up. Adjust with a little more tamarind water or a splash of plain water.
For the tempering, heat the remaining 2 tbsp oil in a small pan and crackle the mustard and cumin seeds, then add the dried red chillies and curry leaves and let them spit for 10 seconds.
Pour the tempering over the dalcha, stir once, and scatter with coriander leaves. Rest 5 minutes before serving with bagara rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. It thickens considerably as it sits; loosen with hot water when reheating over low heat, and check the salt again after.

recipes.name: Double ka Meetha
recipes.subtitle: fried bread soaked in saffron milk and cardamom syrup, the wedding-feast pudding

ingredients.qty: 8 slices of white sandwich bread, crusts off, halved diagonally
ingredients.note: day-old bread fries crisper
in place of khoya if you cannot get it

ingredients.qty: a large pinch, soaked in 2 tbsp warm milk

prepNotes: Leave the bread slices out uncovered for a few hours, or overnight, so they dry a little — fresh soft bread soaks up ghee and turns greasy.
Soak the saffron in warm milk for 15 minutes.
Have the milk reduction, the syrup and the fried bread all ready before you assemble; the bread should meet them warm.

steps.text: Boil the milk in a heavy pan and simmer on low for 20 minutes, stirring often, until reduced to about 450ml and noticeably thickened.
steps.tip: Scrape the base every couple of minutes — reducing milk catches easily.

steps.text: Stir the khoya, or the condensed milk, into the reduced milk along with half the saffron milk. Take off the heat.
In a separate pan, dissolve the sugar in the water and boil 5 minutes to a thin one-string syrup, then add the crushed cardamom and the rest of the saffron milk.
Heat the ghee in a kadhai and fry the nuts and raisins briefly until golden. Remove and set aside.
Fry the bread triangles in the same ghee over medium heat, a few at a time, for about 2 minutes a side until evenly deep golden and crisp right through.
steps.tip: Fry them properly crisp — limp bread disintegrates the moment the milk hits it.

steps.text: Drain the fried bread on a rack for a minute so the surface ghee runs off.
Dip each piece into the warm syrup for 5 seconds only, then arrange in a single overlapping layer in a serving dish.
steps.tip: Five seconds, no more. Longer and the bread collapses.

steps.text: Pour the warm thickened milk evenly over the bread and leave it to soak for 15 minutes.
Scatter the fried nuts and raisins over the top and serve warm or at room temperature.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated, covered. The bread softens further overnight, which many people prefer; warm portions for 20 seconds in a low oven, or serve cold.

recipes.name: Dum Ka Murgh
recipes.subtitle: chicken sealed and slow-cooked in a pale almond and fried-onion gravy

ingredients.note: for birista, the fried onion paste

ingredients.qty: a generous pinch, soaked in 2 tbsp warm milk

prepNotes: Marinate the chicken for at least 3 hours, or overnight refrigerated. This is a white gravy with no browning to hide behind, so the flavour has to go in before cooking.
Hang the yogurt in muslin for 30 minutes and discard the whey. Wet yogurt makes a thin gravy that will never thicken without splitting.
Soak the almonds, poppy seeds and melon seeds in hot water for 20 minutes before grinding, and grind with as little water as possible.
Bring the marinated chicken to room temperature 30 minutes before cooking so the dum time is accurate.

steps.text: Fry the sliced onion in the oil over medium heat until deep gold and crisp, 15 minutes. Drain on paper, cool completely, then crush to a coarse paste.
steps.tip: Cool the birista fully before grinding — warm fried onion smears into an oily sludge instead of a paste.

steps.text: Grind the soaked almonds, poppy seeds and melon seeds with 3 tbsp water to a completely smooth paste. Rub a little between your fingers; any grit means keep grinding.
Mix the hung yogurt, birista paste, nut paste, ginger and garlic pastes, green chilli paste, cardamom, pepper, mace, nutmeg and salt into a marinade.
Coat the chicken thoroughly, cover, and refrigerate at least 3 hours.
Heat the ghee in a heavy pan, tip in the whole marinated chicken with all its marinade, and cook uncovered over medium heat 8 minutes, stirring gently.
Lower the heat to minimum, cover with a tight lid, and cook 30 minutes without lifting the lid.
steps.tip: If your lid is loose, seal the rim with a rope of atta dough or lay foil under it. Escaping steam is escaping cooking liquid.

steps.text: Uncover, stir once from the bottom, and check the gravy: it should be thick, pale and clinging, with ghee pooling at the edges.
Stir in the saffron milk and kewra water and cook uncovered 5 minutes more to tighten the gravy.
steps.tip: Kewra is powerful. A teaspoon perfumes the dish; a tablespoon makes it taste of soap.

steps.text: Rest off the heat, covered, 10 minutes, then scatter over the coriander and mint and serve with sheermal or bagara rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. Reheat covered over low heat with a splash of milk, never on high — the yogurt gravy splits above a bare simmer. It does not freeze well.

recipes.name: Gil-e-Firdaus
recipes.subtitle: bottle gourd cooked down in thickened milk with sago, a wedding-table pudding

ingredients.note: weigh after peeling; a young pale gourd is sweeter

ingredients.qty: a good pinch, soaked in 2 tbsp warm milk

prepNotes: Soak the sabudana in cold water for 30 minutes, then drain. Skipping this leaves hard white centres in the finished pudding.
Squeeze the grated bottle gourd lightly and keep the juice; add it back with the milk rather than throwing away the flavour.
This is a slow reduction. Use the heaviest pan you own or the milk will catch and taste scorched all the way through.

steps.text: Fry the grated bottle gourd in the ghee over medium heat 8 minutes, until it loses its raw smell and the volume halves.
steps.tip: Cook off the water now. Wet gourd added to milk gives a thin, vegetal pudding.

steps.text: Pour in the milk and any reserved gourd juice, bring to a boil, then lower to a steady simmer.
Simmer uncovered 25 minutes, stirring every few minutes and scraping the base and sides, until the milk has reduced by about a third.
steps.tip: Scrape the bottom with a flat spatula, not a spoon. Milk solids settle in the corners and burn there first.

steps.text: Add the drained sabudana and cook 10 minutes, stirring often, until the pearls are translucent with no white dot in the centre.
Stir in the condensed milk and sugar and cook 5 minutes, until dissolved and slightly thickened.
Fold in the grated khoya and cook 3 minutes, until melted and the pudding coats the back of a spoon.
Take off the heat and stir in the ground cardamom, saffron milk and rose water.
steps.tip: Add the rose water off the heat. Boiled, its perfume disappears and only a faint soapiness stays.

steps.text: Stir in half the slivered almonds and pistachios and cool 20 minutes.
Chill at least 3 hours, then serve cold in small bowls scattered with the remaining nuts. It thickens as it chills.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated in a covered container. Serve cold; it thickens further overnight, so loosen with 2-3 tbsp cold milk before serving. Do not freeze.

recipes.name: Haleem
recipes.subtitle: Wheat, lentils and mutton pounded together for hours into a smooth, savoury porridge

ingredients.note: haleem is not a lean dish

prepNotes: Haleem is Ramadan food, cooked in enormous pots and beaten with a wooden paddle until no individual grain or fibre remains. At home, a hand blender does the same job.
Do not blend it completely smooth — it should be homogenous but still have body.

steps.text: Pressure cook the soaked dalia and the mixed dals with turmeric and plenty of water until collapsing, about 5 whistles.
Separately, cook the mutton with ginger, garlic, chilli powder, half the birista and salt until it falls off the bone. Reserve the stock.
Pick the meat off the bones and shred it finely; discard the bones but keep every drop of stock.
Combine meat, grain and stock in a wide heavy pot. Now beat and mash over low heat for 45-60 minutes, adding ghee in stages.
steps.tip: This is the recipe. Under-beaten haleem tastes like lentil soup with meat in it.

steps.text: When it pulls away from the sides of the pot in a single mass, stir in garam masala and mint.
Serve topped with birista, fried mint, ginger julienne and a lot of lemon.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and thickens to a solid block; loosen with hot water and a little ghee when reheating. Freezes 2 months.

recipes.name: Hyderabadi Chicken 65
recipes.subtitle: twice-fried chilli chicken finished in a spitting curry-leaf and yogurt tempering

ingredients.note: thigh stays juicy where breast dries out

ingredients.qty: 4 tbsp, thick, plus 3 tbsp for the finish

ingredients.note: for colour without punishing heat
helps the coating cling
generous — they are half the dish

prepNotes: Marinate the chicken for at least 2 hours, or overnight in the fridge — an hour is not enough for the yogurt to do its work.
Bring the marinated chicken back to room temperature for 20 minutes before frying, or the oil temperature will crash.
Pat the curry leaves completely dry; wet leaves turn hot oil into a volcano.

steps.text: Mix the chicken with the 4 tbsp yogurt, ginger and garlic pastes, kashmiri chilli, chilli powder, garam masala, black pepper, lemon juice and salt. Refrigerate at least 2 hours.
Half an hour before cooking, work the rice flour, besan and beaten egg into the marinade. It should coat each piece in a thin paste, not a batter.
steps.tip: Add the flours late — mixed in early they draw water out and go sludgy.

steps.text: Heat the frying oil in a kadhai to 170C. A cube of chicken should sizzle steadily and rise within 3 seconds.
Fry in three batches, 4-5 minutes each, until pale gold and just cooked through. Drain on a rack, not paper.
steps.tip: Crowding the pan drops the oil temperature and gives soggy, greasy chicken.

steps.text: Raise the oil to 190C and return all the chicken for a second fry of 1-2 minutes until deep red-gold and crisp at the edges. Drain.
Pour off the frying oil, leaving 2 tbsp in the pan. Drop in the curry leaves and slit green chillies and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Whisk the remaining 3 tbsp yogurt smooth, take the pan off the heat and stir it in.
steps.tip: Off the heat, always — yogurt added to a hot pan splits into curds and whey.

steps.text: Return the pan to a low flame, add the fried chicken and toss for 1 minute until every piece is coated and the yogurt has almost dried onto it.
Finish with coriander leaves and serve hot with raw onion rings and lemon.

recipes.storage: Best within the hour — it softens as it sits. Leftovers keep 2 days refrigerated; crisp them again in a hot dry pan or a 200C oven for 6 minutes rather than a microwave.

recipes.name: Hyderabadi Dum Biryani
recipes.subtitle: Kachchi biryani: raw marinated mutton layered under rice and sealed from the start

ingredients.note: only seals the lid and is discarded, so the dish stays gluten-free

prepNotes: Kachchi means raw: the mutton goes in uncooked and must finish in the same time as the rice. That only works with a long marination and a tender cut.
Marinate at least 6 hours, ideally overnight. This is the single biggest determinant of success.

steps.text: Marinate the mutton with yogurt, ginger, garlic, chilli, turmeric, garam masala, half the birista, half the herbs, lemon juice and salt. Refrigerate 6 hours or overnight.
Bring the marinated meat to room temperature and spread it in a heavy pot with 3 tbsp ghee.
Boil the rice in well-salted water with the whole spices until 70% done, then drain immediately.
steps.tip: A firm core in the grain. It finishes on dum.

steps.text: Layer the rice over the raw meat. Top with the remaining birista, herbs, saffron milk and ghee.
Seal with a dough rope or tight foil. Cook on high for 5 minutes to build steam, then on the lowest heat for 45 minutes.
Rest 15 minutes before opening. Serve with mirchi ka salan and dahi chutney.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. Reheat covered with a splash of water. The rice suffers in the freezer.

recipes.name: Hyderabadi Kheema
recipes.subtitle: minced mutton with peas, dry and heavily spiced, the weeknight standby

ingredients.note: goat mince; lamb works and is fattier

prepNotes: If the mince is frozen, thaw it fully and squeeze out the water — wet mince boils instead of browning.
Chop the onions fine and evenly; coarse pieces stay crunchy in a dish that should be uniform.
Have the peas ready to go in at the twenty-minute mark, not at the start.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai and crackle the cumin seeds for 15 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and fry over medium heat for 10 minutes until golden brown and shrunk to a third of its volume.
steps.tip: Take the full ten minutes. Pale onion gives a thin, watery kheema.

steps.text: Stir in the ginger and garlic pastes and the green chillies and cook 1 minute until the raw smell lifts.
Add the mince and break it apart with the back of a spoon. Fry on high for 6-7 minutes until it is uniformly brown with no clumps.
steps.tip: Keep breaking it up in the first two minutes or it sets into lumps you cannot fix later.

steps.text: Add the turmeric, chilli powder, coriander powder, cumin powder and salt and fry 2 minutes.
Add the chopped tomatoes and cook 6-7 minutes until they melt down and oil beads at the edges of the pan.
Pour in the water, add the diced potato if using, cover and simmer on low for 15 minutes.
Add the peas, cover and cook 8 minutes more until the mince is tender and the liquid has almost gone.
Uncover and fry on medium for 4 minutes, stirring, until the kheema is dry and glistening rather than saucy.
steps.tip: Hyderabadi kheema is dry — do not stop while there is still gravy in the pan.

steps.text: Stir in the garam masala, mint, coriander and lemon juice and rest 5 minutes before serving with roti or pav.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and freezes well for 2 months. Reheat in a pan with 2 tbsp water over medium heat, breaking it up as it warms.

recipes.name: Hyderabadi Khichdi
recipes.subtitle: loose rice and moong dal cooked with whole spices, the city's breakfast plate

ingredients.qty: 200g short or medium grain, rinsed till the water runs clear

ingredients.note: the dish is defined by it; oil gives a flatter result

prepNotes: Soak the rice and dal together for 20 minutes, then drain well. This is what gives the grains their soft, separate texture.
Hyderabadi khichdi is eaten with khatta and kheema, so it is deliberately mild. Resist the urge to load it with spice powders.
Measure the water precisely: this khichdi should be loose and grainy, not a porridge.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a pressure cooker and crackle the cumin, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, peppercorns and bay leaf for 40 seconds.
Add the sliced onion and fry over medium heat 8 minutes, until light golden.
steps.tip: Stop at light gold, not brown. Dark onion muddies the pale colour this dish is supposed to have.

steps.text: Add the ginger and green chillies and fry 1 minute.
Stir in the drained rice and dal and fry 3 minutes, until the grains look glossy and smell nutty.
steps.tip: Frying the grains in ghee before the water goes in is what keeps them separate rather than sticky.

steps.text: Add the turmeric, salt and 900ml water, and stir once.
Close the cooker and cook on medium for 2 whistles, then turn off the heat and let the pressure release naturally, about 10 minutes.
Open up and fluff with a fork. The grains should be soft and just holding their shape, with no free liquid at the bottom.
Rest covered 5 minutes, then serve hot with khichdi ka khatta and a spoon of extra ghee.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. It firms up cold; reheat with 3-4 tbsp hot water in a covered pan over low heat, breaking up lumps with a fork.

recipes.name: Khatti Dal
recipes.subtitle: everyday toor dal made unapologetically sour with tamarind

ingredients.qty: 200g, rinsed until the water runs clear

ingredients.note: use a compounded-free asafoetida to keep the dish gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the toor dal 20 minutes if you have the time — it cooks softer and faster.
Soak the tamarind in hot water for 20 minutes, squeeze it out with your fingers and strain; the dal should be assertively sour, not merely tangy.
Most block asafoetida is cut with wheat flour, so buy a compounded-free one if gluten matters to you.

steps.text: Pressure cook the dal with the turmeric, chopped tomato, green chillies and 700ml water for 4 whistles, about 12 minutes.
Let the pressure fall on its own, then whisk the dal hard for 30 seconds until it is smooth and creamy with no whole lentils left.
steps.tip: Whisking, not blending — a blender makes it gluey.

steps.text: Return the pan to a low flame, add the remaining water and salt, and bring to a gentle simmer.
Stir in the tamarind water and simmer 8 minutes, until the raw sour smell has cooked off and the dal has thickened slightly.
steps.tip: Taste after these 8 minutes, not before — tamarind mellows as it cooks.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a small pan for the tempering. Crackle the mustard seeds, then the cumin and fenugreek.
Add the crushed garlic and fry until it turns golden, about 1 minute, then the dried red chillies, curry leaves and asafoetida. It will spit hard.
steps.tip: Take the pan off the heat before the asafoetida goes in — it scorches in seconds.

steps.text: If using onion, add it to the tempering and fry 3 minutes until soft and translucent.
Pour the tempering into the dal, cover immediately for a minute to trap the aroma, then stir through.
Finish with coriander leaves and serve with plain rice and a wedge of lime.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. It sets firm when cold — reheat with 100ml water per portion, stirring until it flows again, and refresh with a small second tempering if it tastes flat.

recipes.name: Khichdi Ka Khatta
recipes.subtitle: thin, sharp tamarind sauce poured over khichdi, sour first and sweet after

ingredients.note: a scant quarter; more turns it bitter
use compounded-free hing to keep the dish gluten-free
balances the sourness; the khatta should still lead with tamarind

prepNotes: Soak the tamarind in hot water for 20 minutes, then squeeze it out thoroughly with your fingers and strain. Do this before anything else.
Khatta is meant to be pourable, closer to rasam than to chutney. Have extra hot water ready in case it tightens too much.
Grate the jaggery before you start; a solid lump will not dissolve evenly in a thin sauce.

steps.text: Squeeze the soaked tamarind hard in its water, strain through a sieve, and press the pulp to get everything out. Discard the fibres.
Heat the oil in a pan and pop the mustard seeds, 20 seconds, until they stop jumping.
Add the cumin, fenugreek seeds and dried red chillies and fry 15 seconds, no longer.
steps.tip: Fenugreek burns in seconds and takes the whole pot bitter with it. Count it out.

steps.text: Add the asafoetida, curry leaves, crushed garlic and green chillies and fry 1 minute, until the garlic is pale gold and the leaves are crisp.
Stir in the turmeric and chilli powder off the heat for 10 seconds so they bloom without scorching.
Pour in the strained tamarind water and 200ml plain water, add the salt, and bring to a boil.
Simmer uncovered 12 minutes, until the raw edge of the tamarind has gone and the sauce smells rounded rather than sharp.
steps.tip: Undercooked tamarind tastes metallic. Twelve minutes is the minimum, and it is the difference between good khatta and puckering acid.

steps.text: Stir in the jaggery and simmer 3 minutes more, until dissolved. Taste: sour should lead, sweet should follow.
Slacken with hot water if it has thickened past pouring consistency, scatter the coriander, and serve hot over khichdi.

recipes.storage: Keeps 5 days refrigerated and the flavour improves after a day. Reheat on the stovetop, thinning with a little hot water as it will have thickened.

recipes.name: Lukhmi
recipes.subtitle: square flaky pastries filled with spiced mutton mince, the classic wedding starter

ingredients.note: the shortening that gives the flaky layers

prepNotes: Rest the dough at least 30 minutes under a damp cloth; unrested dough springs back and will not roll thin.
Cook the mince filling ahead and cool it completely — warm filling steams inside the pastry and bursts the seams in the fryer.
The filling must be dry. Any liquid left in it will make the lukhmi split open in the oil.

steps.text: Rub the melted ghee into the maida with your fingertips for 3 minutes until the flour holds its shape when squeezed in a fist.
steps.tip: This step is the flakiness. Skimp on it and you get a bread, not a pastry.

steps.text: Add the salt and cold water a little at a time and bring together into a firm, tight dough — firmer than a chapati dough. Knead 5 minutes, cover and rest 30 minutes.
For the filling, heat 2 tbsp oil and fry the chopped onion for 8 minutes until golden.
Add the ginger and garlic pastes and green chillies, cook 1 minute, then the mince. Break it up with the back of a spoon and fry on high for 5 minutes until it loses its pink.
Add the turmeric, chilli powder, coriander powder and salt and cook on medium for 12 minutes, stirring, until the mince is dry and the fat has separated out.
steps.tip: Keep going until the pan base stays clear when you drag a spoon through.

steps.text: Stir in the garam masala, black pepper, lemon juice, mint and coriander. Spread on a plate and cool completely.
Divide the dough into 12. Roll each into a 12cm square about 2mm thick, keeping the rest covered.
Put 1.5 tbsp of filling on one half of each square, brush the edges with water, fold into a rectangle and press the edges firmly, then crimp with a fork.
steps.tip: Press out every air pocket — trapped air expands and splits the pastry in the oil.

steps.text: Heat the frying oil to 160C. It should be moderate, not fierce: a scrap of dough should rise slowly over 4-5 seconds.
Fry 4 at a time for 6-7 minutes, turning once, until pale biscuit-gold and blistered. Drain on a rack.
steps.tip: Low and slow is what makes them flaky; hot oil browns the outside while the layers inside stay doughy.

steps.text: Serve hot with sliced onion and lemon.

recipes.storage: Best eaten within a couple of hours. They keep 2 days in an airtight tin and crisp up again in a 180C oven for 8 minutes. Uncooked assembled lukhmi freeze well for a month and fry from frozen at 150C.

recipes.name: Marag
recipes.subtitle: thin white mutton soup enriched with cashew and yogurt, drunk before a biryani

ingredients.note: the bones make the broth
marag is white and chilli-hot, not red
for a richer finish

prepNotes: Soak the cashews, almonds and poppy seeds in warm water for 20 minutes, then grind to a completely smooth paste with a little of the soaking water.
Whisk the yogurt until it is perfectly smooth and leave it at room temperature — cold yogurt splits the moment it hits the pot.
Ask for mutton with marrow bones included; marag without them is just a thin curry.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a pressure cooker and add the cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, bay leaf and mace. Let them puff for 30 seconds.
Add the sliced onion and cook 8 minutes until soft and pale gold — stop before it browns, or the broth loses its whiteness.
steps.tip: Colour in the onion means colour in the soup. Pale gold is the target.

steps.text: Stir in the ginger and garlic pastes and the slit green chillies and cook 1 minute.
Add the mutton and sear on high for 5 minutes until the outside is sealed and no pink shows.
Take the pot off the heat, wait a minute, then fold in the whisked yogurt in three additions, stirring continuously.
steps.tip: Off the heat and in stages — this is the one step where marag most often curdles.

steps.text: Return to a low flame and cook 5 minutes until the yogurt tightens around the meat and no longer smells raw.
Add the water, salt and half the mint. Pressure cook for 5 whistles, about 25 minutes, and let the pressure fall on its own.
Open, and stir in the ground cashew and almond paste. Simmer uncovered 12 minutes until the broth thickens just enough to coat a spoon.
steps.tip: Stir the base often here — nut paste sinks and catches.

steps.text: Add the crushed black pepper and the cream, if using, and simmer 3 minutes more. Marag should stay drinkable, not stew-thick; loosen with hot water if needed.
Finish with the remaining mint and the coriander leaves, and serve in cups with lemon wedges to squeeze in.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. Reheat gently over low heat without letting it boil, since a hard boil splits the yogurt; thin with hot water and re-check the salt and pepper before serving.

recipes.name: Methi Murgh
recipes.subtitle: chicken braised with fresh fenugreek, bitter-sweet and thick rather than soupy

ingredients.note: thigh and drumstick hold up better than breast
deepens the fenugreek note at the end

prepNotes: Toss the picked methi leaves with 1 tsp salt, leave 20 minutes, then squeeze out the dark liquid hard. This is what stops the dish turning harshly bitter.
Take the yogurt out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead. Cold yogurt splits the moment it hits a hot pan.
Pat the chicken dry so it browns instead of steaming.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a kadhai and fry the sliced onion over medium heat until evenly golden brown, 12-14 minutes.
steps.tip: Stir every couple of minutes and take it to gold, not mahogany — burnt onion turns the gravy bitter and there is no rescuing it.

steps.text: Add the ginger and garlic pastes and fry 2 minutes, until the raw smell goes and the oil looks clear at the edges.
Add the chicken and green chillies and sear over high heat 5 minutes, until the pieces are opaque all over.
Lower the heat, stir in the turmeric, chilli powder, coriander and cumin powders with 2 tbsp water, and fry 3 minutes until the oil separates.
steps.tip: The splash of water keeps the ground spices from scorching in the few seconds before the chicken juices come out.

steps.text: Take the pan off the heat for 30 seconds, whisk in the yogurt a spoonful at a time, then return to low heat and cook 5 minutes.
steps.tip: Off the heat and a spoon at a time — this is the only reliable way to keep yogurt from curdling into grains.

steps.text: Fold in the squeezed methi leaves and salt, and cook uncovered 8 minutes, until the leaves collapse and darken.
Cover and simmer on low 12 minutes, stirring twice, until the chicken is tender and the gravy clings to the pieces.
Uncover and cook off any watery liquid over medium heat, 3-4 minutes. Methi murgh should be thick enough to scoop, not ladle.
Sprinkle over the garam masala and crushed kasuri methi, spoon on the ghee, and rest covered 5 minutes off the heat.
Finish with coriander leaves and lemon juice, and serve with rumali roti or plain rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and tastes better on day two. Reheat gently on the stovetop with 2 tbsp water; the microwave dries the chicken out.

recipes.name: Mirchi ka Salan
recipes.subtitle: long green chillies in a thick peanut, sesame and tamarind gravy

ingredients.qty: 10 large mild bhavnagri, slit lengthways, seeds scraped out
ingredients.note: the fat pale ones, not the thin hot ones
the backbone of the gravy
any more turns the gravy bitter
to round off the sourness
salan is meant to be an oily gravy

prepNotes: Soak the tamarind in hot water for 20 minutes and squeeze out a thick pulp; strain and keep the liquid.
Slit the chillies down one side and scrape out the seeds and ribs with a teaspoon handle — that is where nearly all the heat sits.
Dry-roast the peanuts, sesame and coconut ahead and let them cool fully before grinding, or the paste turns oily and grainy.

steps.text: Dry-roast the peanuts in a kadhai over medium heat for 5 minutes until the skins blister and loosen, then rub off the skins in a cloth.
Roast the sesame in the same pan for 1 minute until it pops, then the dried coconut for 1 minute until it smells nutty and turns pale gold. Cool completely.
Grind the peanuts, sesame and coconut with 150ml water to a fine, smooth paste. Set aside.
steps.tip: Grind for longer than you think — any grit here stays gritty in the finished dish.

steps.text: Heat 3 tbsp of the oil and fry the slit chillies for 2-3 minutes, turning, until the skins blister and go khaki. Lift them out and reserve.
In the same oil, fry the chopped onion until soft and light brown, about 8 minutes, then cool and grind to a paste.
Add the rest of the oil to the pan and crackle the cumin, mustard, fenugreek and nigella, then throw in the curry leaves.
steps.tip: The fenugreek should barely change colour — dark fenugreek is bitter.

steps.text: Add the ginger and garlic pastes and fry 1 minute until the raw smell goes, then the onion paste, turmeric, chilli powder and coriander powder. Cook 3 minutes.
Stir in the ground peanut-sesame paste and fry on medium-low for 8-10 minutes, stirring often, until the mixture darkens and oil rises around the edges.
steps.tip: This is the step that decides the dish. Undercooked paste tastes raw and chalky.

steps.text: Pour in the tamarind water and the remaining water, add salt and the jaggery, and simmer uncovered 12 minutes until glossy and the thickness of pouring cream.
Slide the fried chillies back in, cover and simmer 5 minutes more, then rest off the heat 10 minutes and scatter with coriander leaves.
steps.tip: The chillies should stay whole — stir gently or not at all once they are back in.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and tastes better on day two. The oil sets on top when cold; warm it gently on the stove and stir it back in, adding a splash of water if it has tightened.

recipes.name: Murgh do Pyaza
recipes.subtitle: chicken cooked with onions twice over, once browned to a paste and once in chunks

ingredients.qty: 600g total: 3 sliced for browning, 2 quartered into petals

prepNotes: Marinate the chicken in the yogurt with half the ginger-garlic paste, the turmeric and salt for at least 1 hour, refrigerated.
Take the marinated chicken out 20 minutes before cooking so it is not fridge-cold when it hits the pan.
Cut the second lot of onions into petals rather than slices — they need to keep their shape to the end.

steps.text: Heat 3 tbsp oil and fry the sliced onions over medium heat for 12-14 minutes until evenly deep brown. Lift out half and reserve for the finish.
steps.tip: Deep brown, not black. Pull them the moment they go the colour of dark toffee — they keep darkening off the heat.

steps.text: Cool the remaining browned onions and grind to a paste with a splash of water.
In the same pan, add the whole spices — cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, bay leaf — and let them puff for 30 seconds.
Add the remaining ginger and garlic pastes and cook 1 minute until the raw edge disappears.
Add the marinated chicken and sear on high for 6 minutes, turning, until the yogurt has tightened around the pieces and the base looks dry.
steps.tip: Keep the flame high here so the yogurt reduces rather than boils and splits.

steps.text: Stir in the browned onion paste, chilli powder, coriander powder and cumin powder. Fry on medium for 6-8 minutes until oil separates at the sides.
Pour in the water, add the green chillies, cover and simmer 15 minutes until the chicken is tender and pulling from the bone.
Heat the last 2 tbsp oil in a separate pan and sear the onion petals on high for 3 minutes until charred at the edges but still crunchy inside.
steps.tip: This second onion should have bite — that contrast is the whole point of do pyaza.

steps.text: Fold the seared petals, the reserved browned onions, garam masala and black pepper into the curry and cook uncovered 3 minutes to thicken.
Take off the heat, stir in the lemon juice, mint and coriander, and rest 5 minutes before serving with roti.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. Reheat gently on the stove with 3 tbsp water; the onion petals soften on reheating, so add a few freshly seared ones if you want the texture back.

recipes.name: Mutton Do Pyaza
recipes.subtitle: mutton with onion twice over, once melted into the gravy and once in soft wedges

ingredients.qty: 5 medium, three finely sliced and two quartered into petals

prepNotes: Marinate the mutton in the yogurt, ginger and garlic pastes, turmeric and salt for 1 hour at room temperature, or 4 hours refrigerated.
Cut the second lot of onion into quarters and separate the layers into petals. These go in late and must stay in recognisable pieces.
Take the whole spices out of the jar and count them out before you start; the tempering takes 40 seconds and there is no time to hunt.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pressure cooker and crackle the cardamoms, cloves, cinnamon and bay leaf for 30 seconds, until fragrant.
Add the sliced onion and fry over medium heat until deep golden brown, 14 minutes. This lot is meant to disappear into the gravy.
steps.tip: Brown these properly. Pale onion gives a thin, sharp gravy that no amount of simmering will fix.

steps.text: Tip in the marinated mutton and sear over high heat 6 minutes, until the pieces have coloured and the yogurt has dried onto them.
Add the chilli powder, coriander and cumin powders and fry 3 minutes, until the oil separates and the masala smells toasted rather than raw.
Add the tomatoes and green chillies and cook 5 minutes, until the tomatoes break down completely.
Pour in 250ml water, close the cooker and cook on high for 5 whistles, then on low for 10 minutes. Let the pressure drop on its own.
steps.tip: Natural release, always. Forcing the pressure out toughens mutton that was almost tender.

steps.text: Open up, taste for salt, and boil uncovered 5 minutes to reduce the gravy to a coating consistency.
In a separate pan, fry the onion petals in 1 tbsp of the oil skimmed from the curry over high heat, 3 minutes, until browned at the edges but still firm.
Fold the petals into the curry, sprinkle over the garam masala, cover and rest off the heat 5 minutes.
Scatter with coriander leaves and serve with roti or khatti dal and rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated or 2 months frozen. Reheat on the stovetop with a splash of water; the onion petals soften on day two, which is no bad thing.

recipes.name: Patthar Ka Gosht
recipes.subtitle: thin mutton slices seared hard and fast, smoky at the edges and still juicy

ingredients.qty: 600g leg, sliced into 5mm escalopes and flattened
ingredients.note: ask the butcher for boneless leg cut thin
the tenderiser; skip only if using very young meat

ingredients.qty: 1, half in the marinade and half to serve

prepNotes: Marinate 2 hours refrigerated, and no longer than 3. Papaya keeps working, and overnight it turns the meat pasty.
Flatten each slice between two sheets of cling film with a rolling pin until about 4mm thick. Even thickness matters more than any spice here.
Bring the meat to room temperature 20 minutes before cooking, or the outside chars before the centre is done.

steps.text: Grind the green chillies, coriander leaves and mint with 1 tbsp water to a coarse green paste.
Mix the papaya paste, yogurt, ginger and garlic pastes, green paste, pepper, garam masala, cumin, chilli powder, juice of half a lemon and salt.
Coat the flattened mutton slices in the marinade, cover, and refrigerate 2 hours.
Heat a heavy tawa or cast-iron griddle over high heat for a full 5 minutes, until a drop of water skitters and vanishes.
steps.tip: A properly hot griddle is the whole dish; the name comes from cooking it on a heated stone slab. A lukewarm pan stews the meat grey.

steps.text: Brush the griddle with ghee and lay on the slices in a single layer, shaking off excess marinade. Do not crowd the pan.
steps.tip: Work in batches of three or four. Crowding drops the temperature and floods the pan with marinade.

steps.text: Sear 2 minutes without moving them, until the underside is browned and lifts cleanly.
Flip, dot with a little more ghee, and cook 2 minutes more. The slices should feel springy, not firm.
Move the cooked slices to a warm plate and repeat with the rest, wiping the griddle between batches.
Rest 3 minutes, then squeeze over the remaining lemon and serve hot with sliced onion and mint chutney.

recipes.storage: Best eaten within minutes of leaving the griddle. Cooked slices keep a day refrigerated and are decent in a roti roll; reheat 30 seconds a side on a hot tawa, never in a microwave.

recipes.name: Qubani ka Meetha
recipes.subtitle: Dried apricots stewed to a glossy compote, served with cream and blanched kernels

ingredients.note: omit to keep it dairy-free
omit for a nut-free version

prepNotes: Use whole dried apricots with stones, not the bright orange sulphured halves. The stones are cracked and the kernels blanched and served on top.
Soak overnight. There is no shortcut that produces the same texture.

steps.text: Soak the apricots in water overnight until plump. Keep the soaking water.
Pit them, reserving the stones. Crack the stones and blanch the kernels; the skins slip off.
Simmer the fruit in its soaking water with the sugar and cardamom over low heat, 30-40 minutes, until it collapses into a thick glossy compote.
steps.tip: Mash some against the side of the pan and leave the rest in pieces.

steps.text: Sharpen with lemon if the apricots were very sweet.
Cool. Serve at room temperature or chilled, topped with cream and the blanched kernels.

recipes.storage: Keeps a week refrigerated and the flavour deepens. Freezes 3 months.

recipes.name: Sheer Khurma
recipes.subtitle: eid morning milk pudding heavy with dates, roasted vermicelli and nuts

ingredients.note: the khurma in the name
for the thick, milky finish

ingredients.qty: a large pinch, soaked in 2 tbsp warm milk

prepNotes: Soak the saffron in warm milk for 15 minutes so it gives up its colour.
Soak the sliced dates in 100ml warm milk for 20 minutes; they plump up and stop drinking the pudding dry later.
Use a heavy-bottomed pan — milk reduced for 30 minutes will scorch in a thin one.

steps.text: Melt the ghee in a heavy pan and fry the almonds, pistachios and cashews for 2 minutes until golden. Lift them out with a slotted spoon.
Add the raisins to the same ghee and fry 20 seconds until they swell and turn glossy, then remove.
steps.tip: They puff and burn within seconds — stand over them.

steps.text: Add the broken vermicelli to the remaining ghee and roast on low for 3-4 minutes, stirring constantly, until evenly reddish-brown and fragrant.
steps.tip: Even colour matters: pale strands stay chewy, dark ones taste burnt.

steps.text: Pour in the milk and bring to a gentle boil, stirring to keep the vermicelli from clumping on the base.
Simmer on low for 20 minutes, stirring every few minutes and scraping the bottom, until the milk has reduced by about a quarter and coats the spoon.
Add the sugar and stir until fully dissolved, about 2 minutes.
Stir in the soaked dates with their milk, the apricots and the grated khoya. Simmer 5 minutes until the khoya melts in with no lumps.
Add the saffron milk and crushed cardamom and cook 2 minutes more; the pudding should be pourable, a little looser than you want it.
steps.tip: It thickens a lot as it cools — pull it off while it still runs freely.

steps.text: Take off the heat, stir in the rose water, and fold through most of the fried nuts and raisins.
Rest 10 minutes and serve warm in small bowls, scattered with the remaining nuts. It is equally good chilled.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated in a covered container. It sets thick when cold; reheat over low heat with 100ml milk per two portions, or serve it chilled as is.

recipes.name: Shikampuri Kebab
recipes.subtitle: soft mince patties with a cool hung-curd filling hidden inside

ingredients.note: binds the mince; nothing else does this job as cleanly
for the filling

ingredients.qty: 1 large, half finely chopped raw for the filling and half sliced

prepNotes: Hang the yogurt in muslin for at least 4 hours, or overnight in the fridge. The filling must be dry and crumbly; wet curd will burst the kebab in the pan.
The cooked mince has to be bone dry before grinding. Any moisture left in the pan becomes a kebab that falls apart.
Chill the shaped kebabs 30 minutes before frying — cold kebabs hold their shape.
Soak the chana dal 30 minutes so it cooks in the same time as the mince.

steps.text: Put the mince, drained chana dal, sliced onion, ginger and garlic pastes, dried red chillies, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, cumin seeds, salt and 250ml water in a pan.
Bring to a boil, then simmer covered 30 minutes, until the dal is soft and the mince is cooked through.
Uncover and cook over medium heat, stirring, until every trace of liquid has gone and the mixture squeaks against the pan, about 8 minutes. Cool completely.
steps.tip: Do not shortcut this. Damp mince is the single reason shikampuri kebabs disintegrate in the ghee.

steps.text: Grind the cooled mixture to a smooth, stiff paste with no added water. Mix in the black pepper, garam masala and lemon juice, and check the salt.
Make the filling: mash the hung curd with the finely chopped raw onion, green chillies, mint, coriander and a pinch of salt.
Divide the mince into 12. Flatten a portion in your palm, place a teaspoon of filling in the centre, and draw the edges over to seal completely.
steps.tip: Seal with wet fingertips and check for cracks before flattening — an open seam leaks curd and the kebab collapses.

steps.text: Press gently into a disc 6cm across and 1.5cm thick. Repeat with the rest and chill 30 minutes.
Heat 2 tbsp ghee on a tawa over medium-low heat and fry the kebabs in batches, 3 minutes a side, until deep brown and crusted.
steps.tip: Medium-low, and turn only once. High heat browns the outside before the crust is strong enough to survive the flip.

steps.text: Drain briefly on paper and serve hot with onion rings and lemon.

recipes.storage: The shaped raw kebabs keep 24 hours refrigerated and fry better cold; they also freeze 1 month between sheets of paper. Fried kebabs keep 2 days and reheat on a tawa with a little ghee, 2 minutes a side.

recipes.name: Tala Hua Gosht
recipes.subtitle: mutton boiled tender then fried dry with black pepper until the masala clings

ingredients.note: the dominant note of the dish

prepNotes: Marinate the mutton with the ginger-garlic paste, turmeric, chilli powder and salt for 1 hour at room temperature, or up to overnight in the fridge.
Crush the peppercorns coarsely in a mortar just before cooking; pre-ground pepper tastes flat and dusty here.
Use a wide pan for the frying stage — the meat needs room to sit in one layer and colour.

steps.text: Pressure cook the marinated mutton with 1 sliced onion, the whole spices and 400ml water for 5 whistles, about 25 minutes.
Let the pressure fall naturally, then check: the meat should give completely to a fork. If not, cook 5 minutes more.
steps.tip: Undercooked mutton will not tenderise once you start frying it — get it right here.

steps.text: Strain, keeping the stock. Boil the stock down separately to about 100ml of concentrated liquid.
Heat the oil in a wide kadhai and fry the remaining sliced onions for 10 minutes until deep golden brown.
Add the green chillies and curry leaves and let them crackle for 20 seconds.
Add the coriander powder and cumin powder and fry 30 seconds, then tip in the drained mutton pieces.
Fry on medium-high for 12-15 minutes, turning the pieces every couple of minutes, until they are browned on all sides and the masala has dried onto them.
steps.tip: This is the whole dish. Turn, do not stir — you want colour on the meat, not a mash.

steps.text: Pour in the reduced stock a spoon at a time, letting each addition dry off before adding the next, until the pan is dry and glossy.
Add the crushed black pepper and garam masala and toss for 2 minutes off the direct heat.
steps.tip: Pepper goes in at the end; cooked long it loses its top notes.

steps.text: Finish with lemon juice and coriander leaves and serve with roti or bagara khana.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. Reheat in a dry pan over medium heat with 1 tbsp water so it steams loose without going soggy; it is meant to be a dry dish, so avoid adding oil.

recipes.name: Til Ki Chutney
recipes.subtitle: toasted sesame and coconut ground with tamarind into a thick, nutty relish

ingredients.qty: walnut-sized lump, soaked in 3 tbsp hot water

prepNotes: Soak the tamarind in hot water for 10 minutes while you toast the sesame.
Toast the sesame in a dry pan and keep it moving. It goes from pale to burnt in about fifteen seconds and burnt sesame is unusable.
Cool everything to room temperature before grinding, or the chutney sweats and sours within a day.

steps.text: Dry-toast the sesame over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, 3-4 minutes, until the seeds turn one shade darker and start popping.
steps.tip: Tip them onto a cold plate the moment they pop, or the residual pan heat keeps toasting them.

steps.text: In the same pan, toast the grated dried coconut 1 minute, until fragrant and just golden. Set aside.
Add 1 tsp of the oil and fry the dried red chillies, garlic and cumin over medium heat 1 minute, until the chillies darken slightly.
Cool all the toasted ingredients completely, about 10 minutes.
Grind the sesame alone first to a coarse powder, then add the coconut, chillies, garlic, cumin, soaked tamarind with its water and salt.
Grind to a thick paste, adding the water 1 tbsp at a time. Stop while it still has a little grain — this is a chutney, not a puree.
steps.tip: Too much water at once makes it loose and it will not tighten again. Add it slowly.

steps.text: Heat the remaining oil, pop the mustard seeds and crisp the curry leaves, 20 seconds, and pour over the chutney.
Fold in the coriander leaves and serve with rice and ghee, or as a side to biryani.
