recipes.storage: Because of the oil and tamarind this keeps 10 days refrigerated in a glass jar, and improves for the first three. Always spoon it out with a dry spoon. Reheat only the portion you need.

recipes.name: More Kuzhambu
recipes.subtitle: sour yogurt curry with ground coconut and cumin, never boiled

ingredients.note: fresh sweet yogurt gives a flat curry
okra or chow chow are the other usual choices
ground with the coconut; this is what stops the yogurt splitting
adds a rounder body to the paste
any more and the curry turns bitter
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the raw rice and toor dal together for 20 minutes so they grind smooth.
Take the yogurt out of the fridge early — cold yogurt hitting a hot pan splits immediately.
Whisk the yogurt with 1/2 cup water until there is no lump left anywhere.

steps.text: Simmer the ash gourd in 1 cup water with the turmeric and salt for 8 minutes, until translucent at the edges.
Grind the coconut, cumin, green chilli, soaked rice and toor dal with 1/2 cup water to a very smooth paste.
steps.tip: Any grit left in the paste will be obvious in the finished curry.

steps.text: Add the paste to the cooked gourd and simmer 6 minutes, until the raw rice smell disappears.
Take the pan off the heat and let it stop bubbling completely, about 2 minutes.
Pour in the whisked yogurt, stirring constantly as it goes.
Return to the lowest possible heat and warm it only until steam rises and it thickens slightly.
steps.tip: The moment it boils, the yogurt curdles into grains. Take it off before you think you should.

steps.text: Check the salt and take it off the heat entirely.
Heat the coconut oil, pop the mustard seeds, add the fenugreek, red chilli, curry leaves and hing.
steps.tip: Fenugreek burns black in seconds — add it after the mustard has finished popping.

steps.text: Pour the tempering over and serve with hot rice and a dry poriyal.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated and gets sourer. Reheat only to warm on the lowest heat, stirring; it will split if it boils.

recipes.name: Mysore Pak
recipes.subtitle: porous gram flour fudge that dissolves in ghee as you bite it

ingredients.note: sifting is not optional — lumps do not come out later

ingredients.qty: 1.5 cups, melted and kept hot on a low flame
ingredients.note: hot ghee is absorbed; cool ghee sits on top

prepNotes: Grease a 20cm tray and keep it next to the stove — you will have about 30 seconds to pour.
Melt the whole quantity of ghee in a separate pan and keep it hot throughout; you add it ladle by ladle.
Sift the besan twice and warm it in a dry pan for 2 minutes so it absorbs ghee readily.
Read the whole method first. Once the sugar syrup is at one-string, there is no pausing.

steps.text: Dissolve the sugar in the water and boil until the syrup reaches one-string consistency, about 6 minutes.
steps.tip: Test by pulling a cooled drop between thumb and finger — a single thread that holds is right.

steps.text: Lower the heat and add the sifted besan in a thin stream, whisking hard so no lumps form.
Whisk until the mixture is smooth and glossy, about 1 minute.
Start adding the hot ghee one ladle at a time, stirring constantly and waiting until each ladle is absorbed.
steps.tip: Adding ghee faster than the batter can drink it gives a greasy, dense slab.

steps.text: Keep going for 12 to 15 minutes as the mixture froths, bubbles and rises in the pan.
Watch for the moment it turns porous and foamy and the last ghee refuses to be absorbed and pools at the sides.
steps.tip: That refusal is the signal. Miss it and the sweet sets hard and chewy.

steps.text: Pour it into the greased tray immediately without scraping the pan and level the top with the back of a ladle.
Wait 4 minutes, then score it into diamonds while still hot.
steps.tip: Score too late and it shatters; too early and the lines close up again.

steps.text: Cool completely for an hour before lifting the pieces out.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 weeks in an airtight tin at room temperature. Do not refrigerate — it goes hard and loses its porous crumb.

recipes.name: Neer Dosa
recipes.subtitle: lacy, paper-thin rice crepes from the coast, soft and faintly sweet

ingredients.note: sona masoori or any short-grain raw rice

prepNotes: Soak the rice 5 hours or overnight. Neer dosa has no fermentation and no leavening, so the soak is what makes the batter grind fine.
Neer means water: the finished batter should be as thin as full-fat milk and run straight off the ladle in a stream.
Season a cast iron tawa properly beforehand. On a poorly seasoned pan these tear every time.

steps.text: Drain the soaked rice and grind it with the grated coconut and 250ml water to a completely smooth batter, 4 to 5 minutes in the blender.
steps.tip: Rub a drop between your fingers. Any grittiness at all means it needs another two minutes.

steps.text: Pour into a bowl, stir in the salt and thin with the remaining water until it is the consistency of thin milk.
steps.tip: This will feel far too thin. It is meant to. A pourable-but-thick batter gives you a chapati, not a neer dosa.

steps.text: Heat the tawa over medium-high until a drop of water skitters across it, then wipe it with a coconut-oil-dipped cloth.
Stir the batter well, then pour a ladleful from a height onto the hot tawa, moving in a spiral from the outside in. Do not spread it with the ladle.
steps.tip: Filling gaps with extra batter is the instinct to resist; a hole or two is the mark of a proper neer dosa.

steps.text: Cover and cook 60 to 90 seconds until the surface loses its wet sheen and the edges lift on their own.
Do not flip. Fold the dosa in half and then in half again with a spatula and slide it onto a plate.
Wipe the tawa with the oiled cloth between each dosa and stir the batter every time, since the rice settles fast.
steps.tip: Stir before every single ladle. The batter separates within a minute.

steps.text: Serve warm with coconut chutney, a jaggery-coconut filling, or a coastal fish curry.

recipes.storage: Best eaten within a couple of hours, stacked and covered with a cloth so they stay pliable. The batter keeps 2 days refrigerated; whisk and re-thin with water before using.

recipes.name: Paruppu Payasam
recipes.subtitle: moong dal pudding sweetened with jaggery and finished in coconut milk

ingredients.note: roasting is what gives payasam its nutty depth
dark jaggery for colour and a deeper taste
the traditional finish; it keeps the sweetness from cloying

prepNotes: Dry-roast the moong dal on low heat for 5 minutes until golden and fragrant, then rinse and drain it.
Melt the jaggery with 1/2 cup water and strain it — jaggery almost always carries grit.
Keep the thick coconut milk aside and do not let it near a boil later.

steps.text: Pressure cook the roasted dal with 2 cups water for 4 whistles until completely soft.
Mash the cooked dal lightly with a ladle, leaving some texture.
Melt the jaggery with 1/2 cup water on low heat, then strain out the sediment.
Add the strained jaggery syrup to the dal and simmer 8 minutes until it thickens and darkens.
steps.tip: Cooking the jaggery into the dal, rather than just stirring it in, is what makes it taste finished.

steps.text: Stir in the thin coconut milk and simmer 3 minutes more.
Take the pan off the heat and let it stop bubbling before adding the thick coconut milk.
steps.tip: Thick coconut milk splits into curds if it boils. Off the heat, always.

steps.text: Stir in the cardamom and dry ginger powder.
Heat the ghee in a small pan and fry the coconut slivers to gold, then the cashews, then the raisins until they puff.
steps.tip: They brown at different speeds, so add them in that order, about 20 seconds apart.

steps.text: Pour the ghee and fried garnish over the payasam and serve warm.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated. It thickens to a paste when cold — reheat gently with 1/4 cup water or thin coconut milk, without boiling.

recipes.name: Pesarattu
recipes.subtitle: a green whole-moong crepe topped with raw onion, ginger and chilli

ingredients.note: just enough for crispness; more and it stops being pesarattu
4 ground into the batter, 2 finely chopped for the topping

ingredients.qty: 1 large, very finely chopped, for topping

prepNotes: Soak the whole moong and rice together for 6 hours or overnight. The skins must be soft enough to grind smooth without being removed.
Pesarattu batter is not fermented — grind it and cook straight away, which makes it a good same-morning breakfast.
Chop the onion for the topping as fine as you can and keep it dry, ready beside the stove.

steps.text: Drain the soaked moong and rice and grind with the whole green chillies, ginger, 1 tsp of the cumin and the salt to a smooth batter, adding water gradually.
steps.tip: Aim for a batter a shade thinner than dosa batter — it should coat the ladle but pour freely.

steps.text: Stir in the remaining cumin seeds whole, for texture.
Heat the tawa over medium-high, then rub it with half an onion dipped in oil.
steps.tip: The onion-rub seasons the pan and stops sticking better than oil alone.

steps.text: Lower the heat slightly, pour a ladleful in the centre and spread outward in a slow spiral to a 22cm round.
Scatter a generous tablespoon of chopped onion, chilli and coriander over the wet surface and press it down with the ladle.
steps.tip: Press the topping in while the surface is still wet or it falls off when you fold the crepe.

steps.text: Drizzle 1 tsp oil around the edge and cook 3 minutes until the base is crisp and speckled brown and the edges curl away.
Flip and cook 1 minute only, just to set the onion.
steps.tip: One minute on the onion side. Longer and the topping burns while the crepe goes leathery.

steps.text: Fold in half and serve hot with allam pachadi or a plain coconut chutney.

recipes.storage: Eat immediately; pesarattu softens as it sits. The ground batter keeps 2 days refrigerated but the green dulls to olive — stir well and use within that window.

recipes.name: Puliyodarai
recipes.subtitle: dark tamarind rice heavy with sesame oil, peanuts and roasted spice

ingredients.qty: 1 cup raw, cooked firm and spread out to cool
large lime-sized ball, soaked in 1.5 cups hot water

ingredients.note: cold-pressed gingelly oil; the dish is built on it
bitter if you use more
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the tamarind in hot water 20 minutes, then squeeze hard and strain — you want about 1.25 cups of thick extract.
Dry-roast the fenugreek, pepper and sesame separately on low heat, cool them, and grind to a coarse powder.
Cook the rice with 1.75 cups water so it stays separate, then spread it out and cool it completely.

steps.text: Heat 4 tbsp sesame oil in a heavy kadhai and pop the mustard seeds.
Add the peanuts, chana dal and urad dal and fry until all three are deep gold, about 3 minutes.
Add the red chillies, curry leaves and hing and fry 20 seconds until the chillies puff.
Pour in the tamarind extract with the turmeric, coriander powder, jaggery and salt — it will spit, so stand back.
Simmer on medium heat for 15 to 20 minutes until the paste thickens, darkens and the oil separates and pools at the edges.
steps.tip: This oil-separation is the doneness test; before it, the rice tastes raw and sour.

steps.text: Stir in the roasted fenugreek, pepper and sesame powder and cook 1 minute more, then take it off the heat.
Fold roughly half the paste into the cooled rice with the remaining 2 tbsp sesame oil.
steps.tip: Add the paste in stages and taste — puliyodarai should be tangy, not punishing.

steps.text: Rest at least 30 minutes before serving so the rice takes on the colour evenly.
steps.tip: It genuinely improves after a couple of hours.

recipes.storage: The tamarind paste keeps 3 weeks refrigerated in a clean jar under a film of sesame oil. Mixed rice keeps 2 days at room temperature.

recipes.name: Rasam
recipes.subtitle: thin peppery tamarind broth, sharp with tomato and crushed pepper

image.alt: A bowl of rasam served with papad

ingredients.qty: lime-sized ball, soaked in 1 cup hot water
3 tbsp, cooked very soft and mashed
ingredients.note: the dal water is what makes it cloudy, not thick
crush just before using
skin on is fine
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
for the tempering

prepNotes: Cook 3 tbsp toor dal with 1 cup water until collapsing, and keep both dal and its water.
Soak the tamarind in hot water for 15 minutes, then squeeze and strain out 1 cup of thick extract.
Crush the pepper and cumin together coarsely in a mortar — powder from a jar tastes flat here.

steps.text: Squash the tomatoes into the tamarind extract with your hand and add the turmeric, rasam powder and salt.
steps.tip: Hand-crushed tomato gives the pulpy body a knife cannot.

steps.text: Simmer this uncovered on medium heat for 8 minutes, until the raw tamarind smell goes and the surface turns matte.
steps.tip: If it still smells sharply sour, give it 2 more minutes.

steps.text: Stir in the crushed pepper and cumin and the garlic, and simmer 2 minutes more.
Pour in the mashed dal loosened with 2 cups of water and the dal cooking liquid.
Bring it to the point where a rim of froth rises at the edges, then take it straight off the heat.
steps.tip: Never let rasam roll to a full boil — it goes dull and heavy.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a small pan, pop the mustard seeds, then add the red chilli, curry leaves and hing.
steps.tip: The seeds must crackle within 5 seconds or the ghee is not hot enough.

steps.text: Pour the tempering over the rasam and cover for 2 minutes to trap the aroma.
Stir through the coriander leaves and serve over hot rice, or in a tumbler alongside.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and tastes better on day two. Reheat only to steaming, never boiling.

recipes.name: Rava Dosa
recipes.subtitle: lacy, brittle semolina crepe you pour rather than spread

ingredients.note: gives the lace its strength

prepNotes: Rest the batter 30 minutes so the rava swells; a fresh batter thickens on you halfway through cooking.
The batter must be as thin as milk — thinner than seems sensible. That is what makes the holes.
Stir the batter from the bottom before every single dosa; the flours settle within a minute.

steps.text: Whisk the rava, rice flour, maida and salt with 2 cups of water until completely lump-free.
Stir in the cumin, pepper, chilli, ginger, curry leaves, coriander and onion.
Add the remaining 2 cups of water and rest the batter 30 minutes.
Check the consistency — it should run off the ladle in a thin stream like full-cream milk.
steps.tip: If it coats the ladle at all, add more water. Thick batter gives a pancake, not lace.

steps.text: Heat the tawa until quite hot, then lower the heat to medium — a drop of water should vanish instantly.
Pour the batter from a height in a ring around the outside, then fill the gaps with a few splashes.
steps.tip: Pour, never spread. A spatula destroys the holes as they form.

steps.text: Drizzle a teaspoon of oil around the edge and over the middle.
Cook undisturbed 2 to 3 minutes until the edges lift by themselves and the surface is dry and golden.
steps.tip: Trying to move it early is how rava dosas tear.

steps.text: Flip and cook 45 seconds, or fold straight out of the pan if you like it very crisp.
Wipe the tawa with half an onion between dosas and stir the batter before each pour.

recipes.storage: The batter keeps 2 days refrigerated; re-thin with water before use. Cooked dosas do not keep — eat them as they come off the pan.

recipes.name: Sakkarai Pongal
recipes.subtitle: rice and moong dal cooked soft in jaggery syrup with cardamom and fried cashew

ingredients.note: dark kolhapuri or paagu vellam, not sugar
this is a ghee dish; do not cut it back
the traditional finishing note alongside cardamom
cooks the rice softer than water alone

prepNotes: Dry roast the moong dal for 3 minutes before cooking it — the raw smell has to go, and it is what makes pongal smell like pongal.
Grate the jaggery rather than chopping it so it dissolves evenly.
Have the ghee warm and ready; cold ghee added to hot pongal seizes into streaks.

steps.text: Dry roast the moong dal in a pan over medium heat for 3 minutes until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker.
Wash the rice and roasted dal together, then pressure cook with the milk and 500ml water for 5 whistles.
steps.tip: Five whistles, not three. Sakkarai pongal wants the grains collapsed, not separate.

steps.text: Let the pressure fall naturally, open, and mash the rice and dal together with a ladle until creamy.
Meanwhile melt the jaggery with 150ml water in a separate pan over medium heat, stirring, then strain through a sieve to remove grit.
steps.tip: Always strain jaggery. Even good blocks carry sand and cane fibre.

steps.text: Boil the strained syrup 4 minutes until it thickens slightly and coats a spoon.
Pour the hot syrup into the mashed rice and stir over low heat for 8 to 10 minutes until the mixture pulls away from the sides of the pan.
steps.tip: Keep the flame low from here on. Jaggery scorches on the base and the burnt taste spreads through the whole pot.

steps.text: Fry the cashews, coconut slivers and raisins in 2 tbsp of the ghee until the nuts are golden and the raisins plump, then tip them in with their ghee.
Stir in the remaining ghee a spoonful at a time, along with the crushed cardamom and dry ginger powder.
Cook 2 minutes more until glossy, then serve warm.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. It sets firm when cold, so reheat with 2 tbsp milk and an extra spoon of ghee, stirring until it loosens back to a soft spoonable mass.

recipes.name: Sambar
recipes.subtitle: Toor dal and vegetables in a tamarind broth, built on freshly ground sambar powder

ingredients.note: sambar onions
or sesame oil

prepNotes: Cook the tamarind broth and the vegetables together before the dal goes in. Vegetables added to dal never take on the sourness properly.
Sambar powder loses its aroma quickly. If yours has been open six months, it is doing very little.

steps.text: Pressure cook the toor dal with turmeric until completely soft, then whisk it smooth.
Simmer the tamarind extract with the shallots, tomato and harder vegetables, the sambar powder and salt for 12-15 minutes.
steps.tip: Cook the raw edge off the tamarind before the dal goes in.

steps.text: Add quicker vegetables like okra for the last 5 minutes.
Stir in the whisked dal and enough hot water to reach a pourable consistency. Simmer 8 minutes; do not boil hard.
Temper mustard seeds, fenugreek, dried chilli, curry leaves and asafoetida in oil and pour it in.
Add jaggery if the tamarind is sharp, finish with coriander, and rest 10 minutes before serving.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and thickens; loosen with hot water. Freezes 2 months, though okra softens.

recipes.name: Thayir Vadai
recipes.subtitle: fried urad dal vadas soaked soft in seasoned yogurt, cold and gently spiced

ingredients.note: use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
thick, fresh and not sour
loosens the yogurt and keeps it mild

ingredients.qty: 1.5 litres warm, for soaking the vadas

prepNotes: Soak the urad dal 3 hours. Any longer and the batter absorbs oil like a sponge.
Grind the batter with as little water as you can manage — ice cold water, a tablespoon at a time.
Whisk the yogurt with the milk and salt an hour ahead and keep it refrigerated so it is properly cold when the vadas go in.

steps.text: Drain the soaked dal thoroughly and grind to a thick, fluffy white batter, adding cold water a tablespoon at a time. A blob dropped in water should float.
steps.tip: The float test is not optional. A batter that sinks makes dense, oily vadas.

steps.text: Beat the batter by hand for 2 minutes to aerate it, then fold in the green chilli, ginger, crushed pepper, chopped curry leaves, asafoetida and salt.
Heat the oil to 170C. Wet your palm, flatten a lime-sized ball of batter on it and make a hole through the centre with your thumb.
Slide the vadas into the oil, 4 at a time, and fry 4 to 5 minutes turning once, until pale gold — not dark.
steps.tip: Fry these lighter than you would a standalone medu vada. They have to soften in yogurt later.

steps.text: Drain on paper, then drop the hot vadas straight into a bowl of warm salted water for 15 minutes.
Lift each vada out and press it gently between your palms to squeeze out the water. It should feel like a wrung sponge.
steps.tip: Squeeze firmly but slowly, or the vada tears in half.

steps.text: Arrange the vadas in a single layer in a shallow dish and pour the cold yogurt-milk mixture over them.
Refrigerate at least 2 hours so the vadas drink up the yogurt and swell.
Just before serving, heat 1 tbsp of the frying oil and crackle the mustard seeds, red chillies and remaining curry leaves, and pour it over.
Dust with chilli powder, scatter the coriander and serve cold.

recipes.storage: Best on the day it is assembled. Keeps 2 days refrigerated but the vadas slump and the yogurt turns sour after that. Never freeze. Serve straight from the fridge.

recipes.name: Thengai Sadam
recipes.subtitle: leftover rice tossed through toasted coconut, dals and curry leaves

ingredients.note: day-old rice, grains separate
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Cook the rice at least 2 hours ahead, spread it on a wide plate and let it cool completely. Warm rice turns this to mush.
Grate the coconut fresh. Desiccated coconut will not give the moisture this dish needs.

steps.text: Spread the cooled rice on a wide plate, sprinkle with salt and 1 tbsp of the coconut oil, and separate the grains with your fingers.
steps.tip: Oiling the rice before anything else is added keeps the grains from clumping later.

steps.text: Dry roast the grated coconut in a kadhai over low heat for 4 to 5 minutes until it just turns pale gold and smells toasted. Set aside.
steps.tip: Stop while it is blonde. Brown coconut tastes of caramel and overwhelms the dish.

steps.text: Heat the remaining coconut oil in the same kadhai and crackle the mustard seeds.
Add the urad dal, chana dal and cashews and fry until all three are golden, about 2 minutes.
Add the red chillies, slit green chillies, ginger, curry leaves and asafoetida and fry 30 seconds until the leaves crisp.
Return the toasted coconut to the pan and stir for 1 minute so it takes up the tempering.
Turn off the heat, tip in the rice and fold everything together gently with a flat spatula.
steps.tip: Fold, do not stir. A spoon breaks the grains and you lose the texture entirely.

steps.text: Cover and let it sit 5 minutes so the flavours settle, then check the salt and serve.

recipes.storage: Keeps a full day at room temperature, which is why it travels so well, and 3 days refrigerated. Bring back to room temperature before eating rather than microwaving, which dries the coconut out.

recipes.name: Tomato Chutney
recipes.subtitle: deep red cooked chutney, tangy and hot, for idli and dosa

ingredients.note: ripe and red, not pink
byadgi for colour, guntur for heat
skip it if the tomatoes are very sour
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Chop the tomatoes coarsely — they break down anyway.
Cool the fried mixture fully before grinding, or the chutney will froth and taste raw.
Keep 1 tbsp of the oil back for the final tempering.

steps.text: Heat 3 tbsp sesame oil and fry the urad dal and chana dal until golden, about 90 seconds.
Add the red chillies and fry 20 seconds until they darken and swell, then lift out the dals and chillies.
steps.tip: Removing them now stops the chillies burning while the tomatoes cook down.

steps.text: In the same oil, cook the onion and garlic until the onion is soft and edged with brown, about 6 minutes.
Add the tomatoes, tamarind and salt and cook on medium heat for 10 minutes.
Keep going until the tomatoes lose all shape and the oil pools red at the sides of the pan.
steps.tip: Underdone tomato is the single reason this chutney tastes thin.

steps.text: Cool the mixture completely, then grind it with the reserved dals and chillies to a coarse paste, no water.
Heat the last 1 tbsp oil, pop the mustard seeds, then add the curry leaves and hing.
Pour the tempering over the chutney and stir it through.

recipes.storage: Keeps 5 days refrigerated in a clean jar — the sesame oil preserves it. Serve at room temperature; it also freezes for a month.

recipes.name: Tomato Pappu
recipes.subtitle: andhra everyday toor dal cooked soft with sour tomato and garlic

ingredients.note: sour tomatoes make the dish
Andhra pappu is meant to be hot
only if the tomatoes are not sour enough
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Rinse the toor dal until the water runs clear, which stops the dal frothing over.
Chop the tomatoes coarsely; they go into the cooker with the dal and melt away.
Crush the garlic with the flat of a knife rather than mincing it — you want soft sweet cloves at the end.

steps.text: Pressure cook the dal with the tomatoes, green chilli, turmeric and 2.5 cups water for 5 whistles.
steps.tip: Cooking the tomato with the dal, not after, is what makes it pappu rather than dal with tomato.

steps.text: Let the pressure drop naturally, open, and mash the dal against the side of the pot until smooth.
Add the salt, chilli powder and tamarind if using, with 1/2 cup water, and simmer 5 minutes.
Adjust with hot water until it pours thickly off the ladle.
Heat the oil in a small pan and pop the mustard seeds, then add the cumin.
Add the crushed garlic and fry until the cloves turn golden at the edges, about 1 minute.
steps.tip: Garlic browned properly here is most of the flavour; pale garlic tastes raw in the dal.

steps.text: Add the onion and fry 3 minutes until soft and lightly browned.
Add the red chilli, curry leaves and hing and let them crackle for 15 seconds.
Pour the tempering into the dal, stir once, scatter the coriander and serve over hot rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and thickens as it stands. Reheat with a splash of water and a fresh squeeze of lemon if it tastes tired.

recipes.name: Upma
recipes.subtitle: soft savoury semolina with crackling dal, ginger and curry leaves

ingredients.note: coarse bombay rava, not the fine idli variety
brightens the whole pan

prepNotes: Dry-roast the rava on low heat for 4 minutes until it smells toasty and moves loosely in the pan, then tip it out.
Boil the water and keep it on a low flame — it must go in hot or the upma turns lumpy.
Have everything chopped before you start; the tempering to the finish takes six minutes.

steps.text: Heat the oil and pop the mustard seeds until they jump and quieten.
Add the urad dal and chana dal and fry until both turn a light red-gold, about 90 seconds.
steps.tip: The dals are what give upma its crunch; pale dal means no texture.

steps.text: Add the cashews, green chilli, ginger and curry leaves and fry 30 seconds until the leaves crisp.
Add the onion and cook until soft and translucent, about 4 minutes — no browning.
Pour in the boiling water with the salt and let it come back to a rolling boil.
Lower the heat and add the roasted rava in a thin steady stream with one hand while stirring hard with the other.
steps.tip: Dumping it in all at once is exactly how you get lumps.

steps.text: Keep stirring for 2 minutes until the mixture pulls away from the sides of the pan.
Cover and steam on the lowest heat for 3 minutes, then turn off and rest 2 minutes.
Fluff with a fork, squeeze over the lemon and scatter the coriander.

recipes.storage: Best within a few hours. Refrigerate up to 2 days and revive by steaming with 2 tbsp water sprinkled over; microwaving dries it out.

recipes.name: Uttapam
recipes.subtitle: thick fermented pancake with onion and tomato pressed into the top

ingredients.note: parboiled idli rice, not raw table rice
helps the ferment and browns the surface
deseeding stops the topping going soggy

prepNotes: Soak the rice and the dal separately — they grind to different textures and must be ground apart.
Ferment the batter 8 to 12 hours in a warm place; in a cold kitchen use a switched-off oven with the light on.
Do not stir the risen batter vigorously before use — fold gently once so it keeps its air.
Chop the toppings fine and keep them dry in a bowl, ready to scatter.

steps.text: Grind the urad dal and fenugreek with about 3/4 cup cold water to a light, fluffy paste.
Grind the rice separately with 3/4 cup water to a batter with a fine sandy grain still in it.
steps.tip: That slight grain is what gives uttapam its body — a silk-smooth batter spreads too thin.

steps.text: Mix the two by hand with the salt, in wide circular strokes, for 2 minutes.
Cover and leave to ferment 8 to 12 hours until risen by half and smelling pleasantly sour.
steps.tip: A batter that has risen and fallen back is over-fermented — use it, but expect a sharper taste.

steps.text: Heat a tawa on medium until a flick of water dances and evaporates in about 2 seconds.
Pour a ladle of batter and spread it only slightly, to a thick round about 12cm across.
steps.tip: Uttapam is meant to be thick — resist the urge to spread it like a dosa.

steps.text: Scatter a handful of onion, tomato, chilli, coriander and curry leaves over the wet surface and press them in with the back of the ladle.
Drizzle a teaspoon of sesame oil around the edge and cook 3 minutes until the base is golden and the top has set matte.
Flip and cook 90 seconds on the topping side to caramelise the onion, then serve straight from the pan.

recipes.storage: The batter keeps 4 days refrigerated and grows sourer each day. Cooked uttapam is best immediately; reheat on a dry tawa, never in a microwave.

recipes.name: Vatha Kuzhambu
recipes.subtitle: dark, oily tamarind gravy with shallots, spiked with fenugreek

ingredients.qty: large lime-sized ball, soaked in 2 cups hot water

ingredients.note: sambar onions; they stand in for the sun-dried vathal
the quantity is not a typo — this curry sits under a layer of oil
the signature bitterness; measure it exactly
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
rounds off the sourness
only if it refuses to thicken

prepNotes: Soak the tamarind in hot water 20 minutes and strain out about 2 cups of extract.
Peel the shallots and leave them whole — they should stay recognisable in the finished gravy.
This curry needs a long slow reduction, so start it before the rice.

steps.text: Heat the sesame oil in a kadhai and pop the mustard seeds.
Add the fenugreek seeds and chana dal and fry 20 seconds until the fenugreek turns reddish.
steps.tip: Fenugreek that goes dark brown makes the whole pot bitter — pull it early.

steps.text: Add the red chillies, curry leaves and hing and let them crackle.
Add the whole shallots and garlic and fry 5 minutes until the shallots are browned in patches and glossy.
Stir in the sambar powder and turmeric and fry 30 seconds in the oil.
Pour in the tamarind extract with the salt and jaggery and bring to a simmer.
Simmer uncovered on low heat for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring occasionally.
It is done when the volume has dropped by a third and the sesame oil floats clear on top.
steps.tip: That floating oil is the whole test. Until it appears, the tamarind still tastes raw.

steps.text: If it is still thin after 25 minutes, stir in the slaked rice flour and cook 2 minutes more.
Rest 10 minutes off the heat and serve with rice, a spoon of sesame oil and a poriyal.

recipes.storage: Keeps a week refrigerated and improves for the first three days — the oil seals it. Reheat gently; do not freeze.

recipes.name: Ven Pongal
recipes.subtitle: soft rice and moong dal loaded with ghee, black pepper and cumin

ingredients.note: roasting is what stops it tasting like plain khichdi
half in the pot, half poured over at the end
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Dry-roast the moong dal on low heat for 4 minutes until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker, then rinse it.
Crush the pepper coarsely in a mortar — whole peppercorns are unpleasant to bite and ground pepper disappears.
Have the ghee tempering ready before the cooker is opened; pongal stiffens as it cools.

steps.text: Pressure cook the rice and roasted dal with 5 cups water and the salt for 5 whistles.
steps.tip: Five cups looks like far too much water. It is not — pongal should be sloppy.

steps.text: Let the pressure fall on its own, then open and mash the mixture with a ladle until it is soft and shapeless.
Keep it on the lowest heat while you make the tempering, stirring so the base does not catch.
Heat the ghee in a small pan and fry the cashews to pale gold, about 40 seconds.
Add the cumin seeds and crushed pepper and let them sizzle for 20 seconds.
steps.tip: Pepper that fries too long turns acrid — 20 seconds, no more.

steps.text: Add the ginger, curry leaves and hing and fry until the leaves crisp.
Pour the whole tempering into the pongal and fold it through.
Check the consistency and loosen with hot water until it falls off the ladle in a thick sheet.
Serve immediately with the remaining ghee spooned over, alongside coconut chutney.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated but sets firm. Reheat with 1/2 cup hot water per portion, mashing until it flows again, and add a spoon of fresh ghee.
